Industry News: LeRobot v0.6.0: Imagine, Evaluate, Improve

📅 07 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1765 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, this fresh release is about closing the robot learning loop: policies that imagine the future before acting, reward models that tell you when your robot succeeds, a deployment CLI that turns failures into training data, and six new simulation benchmarks to measure it all.
  • LeRobot v0.6.0 introduces world model policies (VLA-JEPA, FastWAM, LingBot-VA) that learn to imagine the future, a wave of upcoming VLAs (GR00T N1.7, MolmoAct2, EO-1, EVO1, Multitask DiT), and a new reward models API (Robometer, TOPReward).
  • Industry observers note that the robotics world is asking a significant question: do world models actually help robot policies?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this fresh release is about closing the robot learning loop: policies that imagine the future before acting, reward models that tell you when your robot succeeds, a deployment CLI that turns failures into training data, and six new simulation benchmarks to measure it all. It also brings depth sensing, VLM-powered dataset annotation, custom video encoding, cloud training on HF Jobs, and a much leaner install.

LeRobot v0.6.0 introduces world model policies (VLA-JEPA, FastWAM, LingBot-VA) that learn to imagine the future, a wave of upcoming VLAs (GR00T N1.7, MolmoAct2, EO-1, EVO1, Multitask DiT), and a new reward models API (Robometer, TOPReward). It ships six new simulation benchmarks unified under lerobot-eval, the lerobot-rollout CLI with DAgger-style human-in-the-loop corrections, FSDP training, and cloud training on HF Jobs. Datasets get depth support, an automatic language annotation pipeline, custom video encoding, and up to 2x faster data loading, all on top of a leaner installation.

Industry observers note that the robotics world is asking a significant question: do world models actually help robot policies? v0.6.0 brings three policies to LeRobot to help answer that question. Each one learns to imagine the future as part of its training, and each takes a different path to keep that imagination affordable.

Recent findings suggest that VLA-JEPA teaches a compact VLA (built on Qwen3-VL-2B) to predict the future in latent space while it learns to act: during training, a JEPA world model has to anticipate upcoming frames from the model's own actions. The trick is that the world model then disappears at inference, so you get world-model supervision at zero extra inference cost. Three ready-to-use checkpoints are on the Hub, including a DROID-pretrained base for fine-tuning:.

Check out the VLA-JEPA documentation and the paper to learn more.

LingBot-VA goes one step further: an autoregressive video-action model that predicts future video and actions together, chunk by chunk, and feeds real observations back in to keep its imagination grounded. You can even save what the robot imagined (--policy.save_predicted_video=true) and compare it with what actually happened. Inference runs on a single 24–32 GB GPU. Check out the documentation and the paper for the technical details.

Recent findings suggest that fastWAM asks the question in its paper title: do world action models need test-time future imagination? It pairs a ~5B video-generation expert with a compact action expert in a single network, so the model literally learns to dream its own rollouts. At inference it skips the dreaming entirely and directly denoises action chunks. Fine-tune it from lerobot/fastwam_base, and read more in the documentation.

We upgraded our NVIDIA GR00T integration to GR00T N1.7, the newest open generation of NVIDIA's cross-embodiment foundation model. N1.7 swaps the previous VLM for Cosmos-Reason2-2B (built on Qwen3-VL) feeding a flow-matching action head, and our integration is parity-tested against NVIDIA's original Isaac-GR00T implementation: same inputs, same outputs. Flash-attention is now optional, so pip install 'lerobot[groot]' just works, and you can load NVIDIA's published checkpoints directly.

According to recent reports, GR00T N1.7 replaces N1.5 in LeRobot. If you need N1.5, pin lerobot==0.5.1.

Sources indicate that molmoAct2, the Allen Institute for AI's vision-language-action model, is now ported into LeRobot with the full lifecycle covered: fine-tuning (full or LoRA), evaluation, and real-robot deployment. Ready-made checkpoints with calibration correction baked in mean you can run it zero-shot on an SO-100/101:.

Inference fits in ~12 GB at bf16, and LoRA fine-tuning fits on a single 24 GB GPU. See the MolmoAct2 documentation for the full deployment guide.

Sources indicate that EO-1, a VLA pretrained upstream on interleaved vision-text-action data, joins LeRobot: a Qwen2.5-VL-3B backbone with a flow-matching action head, contributed by one of the paper's own authors. Train it with the standard lerobot-train workflow using --policy.type=eo1. Details in the documentation and the paper.

The Multitask Diffusion Transformer policy brings the TRI Large Behavior Models recipe to LeRobot: a ~450M-parameter diffusion transformer conditioned on CLIP vision and language embeddings, so one model learns many tasks selected via natural language. It supports both diffusion and flow-matching objectives, and it is small enough to train yourself. See the documentation.

According to recent reports, VLAs don't have to be huge. EVO1 packs its policy into 0.77B parameters, an InternVL3-1B backbone with a flow-matching action head, small enough to fine-tune and run in real time on modest GPUs. It ships with two-stage fine-tuning and Real-Time Chunking support out of the box. See the EVO1 documentation and the paper.

Success detection and progress estimation are missing pieces in the robot learning loop, and v0.6.0 gives them a home. LeRobot now has a unified reward models API (lerobot.rewards), mirroring the policies API, with four reward models behind one interface - the HIL-SERL reward classifier, SARM, and two new additions:.

Sources indicate that robometer is a pretrained, general-purpose reward model: point lerobot/Robometer-4B at any LeRobot dataset and it scores task progress and success from raw video plus a language instruction, with no task-specific training required. It is built on Qwen3-VL-4B and trained via trajectory comparisons over a dataset of more than one million robot trajectories (RSS 2026 paper).

Recent findings suggest that TOPReward goes fully zero-shot: no reward weights at all. It wraps an off-the-shelf VLM (Qwen3-VL) and reads the log-probability of the token "True" given the trajectory video and the task instruction. Any capable VLM becomes a reward function.

Sources indicate that both ship with labeling scripts that write per-frame progress curves into your dataset, ready for reward-aware behavior cloning (RA-BC), dataset quality inspection, and progress-overlay videos. Check the Robometer and TOPReward docs.

Recording is no longer stuck with one hard-coded codec. The fresh --dataset.rgb_encoder.* options expose the full encoding surface (codec, quality, pixel format, GOP, presets), and vcodec=auto probes for hardware encoders like NVENC, VideoToolbox, VAAPI, and QSV before falling back to the default software AV1 encoder. For existing datasets, one command re-encodes everything:.

Full details in the video encoding documentation.

Industry observers note that plug in an Intel RealSense, set use_depth: true, and LeRobot records depth maps end to end: captured in millimeters, compressed as compact 12-bit depth video streams alongside your RGB cameras, and decoded back to physical units at training time. Depth renders live during recording and in lerobot-dataset-viz, and it works across SO-100/101, Koch, OpenArm, reBot, Unitree G1 and more.

Your dataset stops being one task string per episode. LeRobot datasets now natively store rich language annotations (timestamped subtasks, plans, memory, corrections, speech, and per-camera VQA pairs), and the upcoming lerobot-annotate CLI fills them in automatically using a VLM that watches your episodes:.

Sources indicate that A YAML recipe layer then renders these annotations into chat-style training messages at sample time: exactly the data tomorrow's long-horizon, talking robot policies will train on. Scale it up with HF Jobs, and read the annotation pipeline docs to learn more.

Training on video datasets is now up to ~2x faster out of the box: multi-camera frames decode in parallel, dataloader workers ship compact uint8 frames (4x less memory between processes), and persistent workers keep decoder caches alive across epochs. Loading a subset of a large dataset (episodes=[...]) went from minutes to milliseconds (275 s down to 0.06 s in our benchmark). Sampling is also deterministic and resumable now, so interrupted trainings restart sample-exact.

v0.5.0 planted the flag on LeRobot as an evaluation hub for VLAs; v0.6.0 makes it the real deal with six newly introduced simulation benchmarks, all runnable through the same lerobot-eval CLI, each with a docs page, a Docker image, and a SmolVLA baseline checkpoint smoke-tested in CI:.

Simulator backends require specific system dependencies with their own install steps; each docs page has the exact recipe, and every benchmark ships a ready-made Docker image if you'd rather skip the setup.

Together with LIBERO, Meta-World, and NVIDIA IsaacLab-Arena, that makes nine benchmark families under one roof, and a latest Adding a New Benchmark guide documents exactly how to plug in yours. Evaluation also got faster: parallel eval now defaults to async vectorized environments, benchmarked at up to 2x faster.

Recent findings suggest that deploying a policy used to be a hack on top of lerobot-record. The newly introduced lerobot-rollout CLI makes deployment its own workflow, with pluggable strategies and inference backends (including Real-Time Chunking for slow compatible VLAs). The base strategy just runs the policy. sentry records continuously, rotating episodes and uploading to the Hub as it goes. highlight keeps a ring buffer and saves the last N seconds when you hit a key, so an interesting moment is never lost. episodic mirrors the classic episode/reset recording workflow. And dagger turns deployment into data collection.

With the DAgger strategy, you watch your policy run, hit a key (or a USB foot pedal) the moment it goes wrong, take over with your leader arm to record the correction, and hand control back. Actuated leaders are driven to the follower's pose before you take over, so the handover is jerk-free. Every correction frame is tagged with an intervention flag, and the resulting dataset is ready for the next fine-tune:.

In a recent development, deploy, collect corrections, fine-tune, repeat: the robot learning flywheel is now a CLI flag. Read the deployment docs.

According to recent reports, robot foundation models are outgrowing single GPUs. LeRobot training now supports FSDP (fully sharded data parallel) through Accelerate: parameters, gradients, and optimizer state are sharded across GPUs, and checkpoints are gathered back into a plain single-file model.safetensors that loads like any other policy. You can even resume an FSDP run on a different number of GPUs. See the multi-GPU training docs.

It has been revealed that no GPU? No problem. The exact same lerobot-train command now runs in the cloud by adding one flag:.

Recent findings suggest that leRobot pushes your local dataset to a private Hub repo if needed, submits the job, streams logs to your terminal, and pushes the trained policy to the Hub at the end. Pick anything from a T4 to 8x H200 with --job.target (compute is billed pay-as-you-go). Check out the documentation.

Check the release notes for the full list and migration pointers for the breaking changes.

Beyond these headline features, v0.6.0 includes hundreds of bug fixes, documentation improvements, and quality-of-life upgrades across the codebase, from smarter defaults to more reliable CI.

In a recent development, we want to extend a huge thank you to everyone in the community. This release includes work from academia, industry and hobbyists teams who chose LeRobot as the home for their models and benchmarks. Every PR and bug report pushes open-source robotics forward.

Recent findings suggest that stay tuned for more to come 🤗 Get started here! – The LeRobot team ❤️.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Motorola has posted an updated list of devices getting its Android 17 patch, with a few updates already available and many more left to go.

With the update now rolling out to select devices, most recently the Razr Fold, Motorola is confirming an official list of devices getting Android 17.

Sources indicate that the list was posted by Motorola Brazil, so this includes devices Motorola doesn’t sell in US markets, and also lists Razr devices without their year naming scheme, rather their international branding – i.e. “Razr (2026)” is “Razr 70.”.

It has been revealed that as per usual, Motorola’s upgrade rollouts may see timing vary by region. The Razr Fold update, for example, is currently rolling out in some international markets but has yet to land in the US.

Here’s the full list of Motorola devices officially confirmed to be getting Android 17:.

Motorola explains what’s new in Android 17 as follows:.

Among the new features of Android 17 are improvements to the system interface, with more customization options, new icons, and changes to the layout of buttons and widgets. The Settings menu has been redesigned to make navigation more intuitive and facilitate access to the smartphone’s main functions.

Artificial intelligence in everyday life.

With the update, Circle to Search now offers real-time translations, allowing you to understand content in other languages ​​more easily, without having to interrupt your current activity on your smartphone.

Simplified connectivity and sharing.

Sources indicate that android 17 enhances connectivity with Instant Hotspot , which simplifies sharing your internet connection between compatible devices. Quick Share has also received improvements to facilitate file transfer, including compatibility with iOS smartphones via QR Code.

According to recent reports, security remains a top priority for the system. The Authentication Failure Lock , a security feature in case of theft, locks the screen after unsuccessful authentication attempts. Meanwhile, Message-Based Fraud Detection enhances the identification of potential threats and fraud. Furthermore, access to emergency calls has become easier and faster.

More control over the visual experience.

It has been revealed that the enhancement also improves HDR brightness control, which adjusts the screen intensity to highlight bright details in compatible photos and videos. Users can adjust this brightness for more comfortable viewing, or even disable the feature.

The Motorola Signature 27, the organization’s newly introduced flagship, ships with Android 17 out of the box.

Run AI workloads on any cloud, store on Hugging Face: zero-egress storage with SkyPilot

📅 07 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1080 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For most teams, models and datasets live in a bucket in one region of one cloud.
  • In a recent development, together with Hugging Face, we've joined the two halves: your models and datasets stay on the Hub, and SkyPilot runs the compute (dev, training, or serving) on whatever cluster has the GPUs.
  • According to recent reports, skyPilot tasks already read and write cloud object stores (S3, GCS, Azure, R2, and many more) by mounting them at a local path.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For most teams, models and datasets live in a bucket in one region of one cloud. The GPUs you can get, whether for development, training, or serving, increasingly sit on a different cloud than your data. The moment those two come apart, you pay a cross-cloud transfer tax just to read your own data onto your own GPUs.

In a recent development, together with Hugging Face, we've joined the two halves: your models and datasets stay on the Hub, and SkyPilot runs the compute (dev, training, or serving) on whatever cluster has the GPUs. Mount a Hugging Face Bucket or any Hub repo into a SkyPilot job with one hf:// URL and the HF_TOKEN you already have, then launch it wherever capacity is. Hugging Face charges no egress, so reading your data onto those GPUs costs nothing, on any cloud.

According to recent reports, skyPilot tasks already read and write cloud object stores (S3, GCS, Azure, R2, and many more) by mounting them at a local path. Hugging Face Storage now joins that list as store: hf, reached through the hf:// scheme:.

Industry observers note that that one hf:// scheme covers the whole lifecycle: read the model and dataset from their repos, write checkpoints to a Bucket while you train, publish the finished model back to a repo, and pull it onto inference servers when you serve. Most teams already keep their models and datasets on the Hub, so there is no migration step and no latest storage account to create.

Sources indicate that MOUNT uses Hugging Face's hf-mount FUSE backend, so a bucket or repo highlights up as a local path next to SkyPilot's other FUSE mounts (gcsfuse, blobfuse2, rclone, goofys). The fetching happens at the filesystem layer: when your code issues a read(), the driver pulls just those bytes from the Xet backend, so only the data you actually touch crosses the network, and hf-mount keeps an on-disk cache so repeat reads stay local. That on-disk cache is the behavior SkyPilot gives its other backends under MOUNT_CACHED, where a plain MOUNT instead streams every read from the bucket with nothing kept locally. For the hf store, MOUNT and MOUNT_CACHED behave the same, so either mode keeps the cache.

Sources indicate that because reads are lazy, a process can start working through a large file before the whole file has downloaded, instead of blocking on a full copy first. That keeps the GPU busy almost immediately, training on data as it streams in rather than sitting idle (and billing) while a dataset or checkpoint copies down. It pays off most on the first epoch, when nothing is cached yet. COPY takes the other route and downloads through huggingface_hub up front, with no special requirements.

It has been revealed that authentication is the token you already have. Set HF_TOKEN in your environment and hand it to a run with --secret HF_TOKEN; SkyPilot uses it for the mount on whatever cloud the job lands. One token works whether the job lands on AWS, GCP, Azure, Nebius, Lambda, or your own Kubernetes cluster, so there are no per-cloud bucket keys to juggle.

Sources indicate that GPU capacity rarely comes from one place anymore. To get enough H100s and H200s, teams hold reserved and committed capacity across several vendors at once (a block on a hyperscaler, a cluster on a neocloud, maybe an on-prem rack) and run wherever they have allocation. SkyPilot is built for this: one job spec, scheduled across 20+ clouds, Kubernetes, and on-prem, landing on whichever reserved cluster is free.

Industry observers note that object storage has been the catch. Object stores are regional and per-cloud, so feeding a GPU or an inference server that sits in a different vendor's data center means either keeping a copy of your data in every vendor's bucket or paying to pull it across. Most clouds charge egress (around $0.09/GB out of AWS) the moment data leaves their network, and often between regions inside one cloud. Pulling a base model onto every inference node, or iterating a dataset for several epochs from a cluster on another cloud, adds a hefty bill on top of GPUs you have already reserved. Teams end up pinning each run to whichever vendor holds the data and leaving the rest of their capacity idle.

Hugging Face Storage takes that cost off the table where it bites: the read side. With no egress or CDN fees and storage at $12-18/TB/month (versus AWS S3 at roughly $23/TB plus egress), the same bucket is reachable from every one of those clusters, and reading from it is free no matter where the GPUs run. Writing back still costs your compute cloud's usual egress, the same as it would to any off-cloud store, but for most AI work the reads dominate: a dataset streamed over many epochs, or model weights pulled onto every latest training or inference node. So you stop pinning each run to whichever vendor holds a copy of the data.

To collect some benchmark numbers, we ran a small fine-tune: Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B on the HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking dataset with TRL's SFTTrainer, mounting the model read-only from its Hub repo and writing every checkpoint to a Hugging Face Bucket. The same SkyPilot YAML ran on AWS, GCP, and Lambda, changing only --infra. SkyPilot placed each job wherever GPUs were free, and all three read and wrote the same bucket.

Per cloud, checkpoints wrote to the bucket at:.

Hugging Face Buckets are built on Xet, which uses content-defined chunking to split files into ~64 KB chunks and store each unique chunk once. Because the boundaries follow the content, an edit changes only the chunks it touches and the rest are recognized as already stored. This pays off in a few places:.

How much you save depends on how much your artifacts overlap, but the deduplication is automatic: you write a checkpoint as usual, and only the newly introduced chunks leave the machine.

Recent findings suggest that add an hf:// mount to any SkyPilot task and launch. MOUNT needs a base image with glibc 2.34+ and /dev/fuse.

It has been revealed that the initial store: hf support started as a contribution from Nikhil Jha. The Hugging Face team carried it forward and upstreamed the hf-mount FUSE fixes that let it mount in unprivileged containers, the default on many Kubernetes clusters. The SkyPilot team wired it into the storage backend. The whole path is open source: SkyPilot, Hugging Face's hf-mount, and the huggingface_hub client.

Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (449 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Googleblog

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Long-context training — including pretraining and post-training, has become a foundation of frontier AI models.
  • In particular, efficient training at multi-million-token sequence lengths runs into the following bottlenecks:.
  • Today, we are excited to announce long-context training support in MaxText, Google Cloud's open-source JAX training framework.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Long-context training — including pretraining and post-training, has become a foundation of frontier AI models. Longer native sequence lengths give large language models (LLMs) the working memory to read a whole code repository or ingest hours of video, and reason through multi-step agentic tasks. In three years, context windows have grown from 128K–200K tokens to 1M–2M, and models trained toward 10M tokens are arriving. Training at those lengths, not just serving them, is where the system limits show up.

In particular, efficient training at multi-million-token sequence lengths runs into the following bottlenecks:.

Today, we are excited to announce long-context training support in MaxText, Google Cloud's open-source JAX training framework. MaxText enables this by supporting four context-parallel strategies on Cloud TPU: All-gather, A2A (DeepSpeed Ulysses), P2P (Ring Attention), and the A2A + P2P hybrid (Unified Sequence Parallelism, or USP), combined with load balancing and sequence packing. All four use the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel. Combined with the 3D inter-chip interconnect (ICI) ( supported on TPUs such as TPU 5p or TPU 7 (Ironwood) ), this lets one sequence span an entire slice while communication overlaps compute and memory per chip stays flat. In our benchmarks, Llama 3.1 8B (25 head dim, 16 query heads) demonstrates exceptional long-context efficiency, achieving 70% Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) on TPU 5p for sequence lengths up to 4 million tokens. Across both TPU 5p and TPU 7, context can be seamlessly extended to 14 million tokens—with TPU 7 consistently maintaining 50% MFU across all sequence scales below 6 million tokens.

This functionality is available today in MaxText v0.2.4(doc).

Context parallelism splits a long sequence across chips, so no chip holds the activations of the whole sequence. Context parallelism can be combined with data and tensor parallelism, and the smallest context-parallel size that fits your sequence in HBM is usually the right one. This also holds for sparser attention variants which cut attention compute but not the activations of every other layer.

Recent findings suggest that attention is the one global operation where every token needs the keys and values of every preceding token, so each context parallel strategy has to bring those keys and values back together. Each makes a different tradeoff between memory (how much KV a chip holds), communication (how much moves per layer, and whether it overlaps compute), and model shape (how many attention heads to split).

It has been revealed that all-gather: Each chip keeps its chunk of the sequence and, at every layer, gathers the keys and values from every other chip. It is the simplest option. However, because causal masking causes later tokens to attend to larger prefixes, All-gather requires balancing compute load across devices.

AI companions are the most demanding consumer use of large language models right now. A coding assistant can forget your last message and still be useful. A companion that forgets your name, your running story, or the plan you made last Tuesday has failed at its one job. On top of that, people now expect voice calls that feel like a phone conversation, not a walkie-talkie exchange with a five-second pause.

Three engineering problems decide whether a companion app works: how much of the conversation fits in the model's context window, what the app remembers once the window fills up, and how fast the voice pipeline answers. Here is how consumer companions handle each one, with real tier and pricing examples, and what developers can take from their designs for their own products.

Most LLM products are judged on single answers. Companions are judged on continuity. That creates pressure in three places at once:.

Every consumer companion is a different set of trade-offs across those three constraints, and the trade-offs are increasingly how the apps are priced.

The context window is the total number of tokens the model can see when it writes the next reply. In a companion app, that budget is spent before the user says anything:.

When the chat log outgrows what is left, the oldest messages fall out. The user experiences this as the companion "forgetting" mid-conversation. This is why context size is now a headline spec in the category, and a paid feature. SpicyChat AI, for example, gives free accounts a 4K context window, then scales memory to 8K on its $19.95/mo tier and 32K on its $29.95/mo tier. Janitor AI runs about 9K of context on its own JanitorLLM. Independent uncensored AI chat benchmarks record these context sizes alongside refusal behavior and pricing, because context length predicts how long a roleplay stays coherent better than any marketing claim.

According to recent reports, some apps sell memory in messages rather than tokens. Fantasy GF's pricing page lists a 60-message base "smart memory" and 5x that, 300 messages, on its Ultra blueprint. Others sell it as a memory multiplier on higher subscription tiers. The pattern is consistent across the category: memory depth is the upgrade lever, not the model itself.

Sources indicate that no consumer app keeps an entire relationship in the prompt. Persistent memory is a separate system that writes to storage and reads back into the context window on each turn. In practice it has three layers:.

Recent findings suggest that the differences users notice are usually retention policies, not algorithms. Crushon AI's own subscription docs say free-initiative chat history is deleted after 7 days of inactivity, while paid aims keep it for the membership period. Paid tiers across the category commonly promise that memories never expire. There is also a security angle worth stating plainly: companion chat logs are among the most sensitive data a consumer product can hold. A 2024 breach at Muah.ai, first reported by 404 Media, exposed roughly 1.9 million users' email addresses together with their private prompts. Any app that builds persistent memory is also building a liability, and developers copying the pattern should treat the memory store as the most protected part of the system.

A voice call in a companion app is three models chained together: speech-to-text, the LLM, and text-to-speech. Run them strictly in sequence and a single reply can take several seconds, which reads as dead air. The apps that feel fast attack each stage the same way:.

According to recent reports, with every stage streaming, time-to-first-audio can land close to a second on a good connection, which is roughly the threshold where a conversation stops feeling laggy. Voice is also expensive to run - three model calls instead of one, plus audio bandwidth - which is why it is metered harder than text. Fantasy GF charges 8 tokens per minute for voice calls (4 on Ultra), which turns the 100 monthly tokens on its entry proposal into about 12 minutes of call time. SpicyChat, for its part, only adds text-to-speech at its top tier. Latency engineering and unit economics are the same problem here: faster pipelines cost less per call, and cheaper calls are what make voice viable below the top plan.

Tier details below come from each app's own pricing or documentation pages, checked November 16, 2026, and cross-checked against il.ly's AI companion testing guide, which hands-tests 15 companion apps across memory, media, and voice.

Two takeaways from the table. First, nobody sells a bigger base model - they sell a bigger window into the same one. Second, the free tiers are deliberately memory-poor: limited context and short retention are the upgrade prompt.

Even if you never build a companion, these apps are a useful reference architecture for any stateful LLM product:.

According to recent reports, consumer AI companions have turned three hard infrastructure problems - bounded context, durable memory, and real-time voice - into their pricing pages. Context size, memory depth, and voice access are the tiers. If you are building anything stateful on an LLM, this category is worth watching closely: it is solving continuity and latency problems at consumer scale, in public, one subscription tier at a time.

Sources indicate that it is the total amount of text, measured in tokens, that the model can consider when writing its next reply. The character definition, stored memories, recent chat, and the newly introduced message all share that budget. When the conversation exceeds it, the oldest content drops out and the companion appears to forget.

Yes, through a memory system separate from the context window. Apps summarize older chats, extract stable facts about you into a profile, and retrieve relevant past moments into the prompt. Retention varies: some free tiers delete chat history after as little as 7 days of inactivity, while paid intends typically keep memory for the membership period.

Sources indicate that A voice turn runs three models - speech-to-text, the LLM, and text-to-speech - instead of one, plus audio transfer. Providers pass that cost on through per-minute token charges or by locking voice behind higher tiers.

In a recent development, for casual chat, 4K to 9K tokens works. For long-running roleplay or a companion expected to hold plot threads for weeks, 32K and up, or a well-built memory layer on top of a smaller window, makes the visible difference.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At Microsoft Build 2026, we unveiled Foundry Managed Compute and Hugging Face models on Foundry — a curated catalog of open-weight models from the Hugging Face ecosystem, refreshed weekly, deployable in one click onto Foundry Managed Compute. Weights are pre-staged in Azure, runtimes are built and scanned by Microsoft, and every model in the Collection ships with the same enterprise security, governance, observability, and billing that applies to every other model on Foundry.

Sources indicate that microsoft Foundry is a platform for building and operating agentic AI applications. Foundry starts with the widest model selection on any cloud — models from Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek, Hugging Face, and others, spanning frontier, open-source, and custom weights — all accessible through a single endpoint and a single set of SDKs in Python, C#, JavaScript, and Java.

On top of those models sits the Foundry Agent Service: multi-agent orchestration with built-in memory, knowledge grounding through Foundry IQ, and a catalog of connectable tools via agentic protocols, so agents can work with enterprise data. Once agents are running, Foundry provides end-to-end tracing, real-time monitoring, continuous evaluations, and a prompt optimizer that improves agent behavior based on eval results — observability and quality loops that are part of the platform.

Alongside that, developers get access to:.

Alongside pay-per-token (lowest-friction path to get started) and provisioned throughput (predictable, high-performance production workloads on frontier models), Foundry Managed Compute is the third deployment option in Foundry: a managed GPU platform-as-a-service for open-source and custom models.

You deploy a model instance described by the things that matter to your workload — parameter count, context length, and whether you want to optimize for latency or throughput — and Foundry handles the GPU topology underneath, whether the instance lands on one accelerator or several, so you think and plan in model terms.

Microsoft takes care of the machine: container updates, runtime upgrades, and security patches happen automatically on the supported runtimes — vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, NIM, TEI, llama.cpp — without redeploying your model, while model configuration, deployment behavior, and routing stay with you.

That consistency carries through the developer surface — pay-per-token, provisioned throughput, and Managed Compute share:.

Open-source models integrate with Foundry Agents the same way frontier models do, so you can mix model types in a single agent without a separate integration path.

Recent findings suggest that same code, same workflow. Quota is aligned to accelerator families, so a strategy built on the H100 family today carries forward as fresh hardware generations come online.

According to recent reports, hugging Face is the public square of open AI: 15 million builders, 400,000 organizations, and over 3 million open models published, with new frontier capabilities — agentic coding, video segmentation, speech, embeddings — landing weekly. It's the GitHub of open models, where the community publishes weights, writes model cards, compares evaluations, and pulls models for experimentation.

Open models have closed the gap with proprietary models on benchmark after benchmark, and they unlock things proprietary endpoints can't:.

According to recent reports, the catch has always been the operational layer: discovery, license review, security screening, runtime selection, GPU sizing, image building, CVE patching, and standing the model up behind an enterprise-grade endpoint. Hugging Face, by itself, is not an enterprise serving platform. Hugging Face models on Foundry is that operational layer, run by Microsoft.

The Hugging Face Collection brings a curated subset of models directly into the Foundry Model Catalog:.

From your side, an open-weight model in the Hugging Face Collection looks and behaves like any other model in the Foundry Model Catalog, and every model in the Collection has been put through a multi-stage publishing pipeline before it ever shows up there.

Hugging Face and Microsoft work together to bring the most popular open-weight models from the Hugging Face ecosystem to Microsoft Foundry — production-ready for enterprise environments — through a systematic curation process:.

Because weights are pre-staged in Azure storage and runtime images live in a Microsoft-managed registry, your deployments won't need outbound network access to Hugging Face Hub — you can deploy to production inside a private network.

Industry observers note that hugging Face models on Foundry are powered by a versatile collection of community-built, open-source inference runtimes — each selected and tuned for Foundry Managed Compute, and matched to the model architectures it serves best. Across all runtimes, the systematic curation process means upcoming versions and patches land on Foundry promptly, and existing model deployments are upgraded automatically — without requiring you to redeploy.

vLLM — the default high-throughput serving engine for open large language models, tuned for production GPU workloads. Because Hugging Face is a direct contributor to vLLM, any model in the Transformers library can run on vLLM out of the box — so when a new model lands on Hugging Face, it can be served on Foundry the same day, with no waiting on a custom integration.

SGLang — a serving engine for language and multi-modal models, with strong support for structured outputs (JSON, regex, grammar-constrained generation) that agentic and tool-using workloads depend on. Hugging Face and the SGLang team have built a Transformers backend integration for SGLang, so any model in the Transformers library runs on SGLang out of the box — and reaches Foundry the same day it lands on Hugging Face.

Text Embeddings Inference (TEI) — the runtime for embedding, reranker, and sequence-classification models. Accelerator-specific images ship with kernels compiled for each GPU and CPU family Foundry supports, keeping the embedding hot path lean for RAG and semantic-search workloads.

llama.cpp — the CPU and small-GPU path for GGUF-quantized models. Useful for cost-optimized deployments, smaller models, and CPU-only regions, with the same OpenAI-compatible API as vLLM and SGLang.

TensorRT-LLM and NIM — used on NVIDIA hardware where NVIDIA's optimized kernels and Triton-based serving deliver meaningfully better latency or throughput for specific model families.

hf-serve — Hugging Face's own multi-model inference server, used for model architectures outside the LLM and embedding fast paths (vision, audio, segmentation, and other Transformers-native pipelines) so the Collection can cover every modality with a consistent serving layer.

The Hugging Face Collection in the Foundry Model Catalog is where you start, and deployment is five steps:.

A deployment template is the unit of choice in step 2: a named, versioned asset that pins the runtime, the accelerator family and count, the context length, and the runtime-specific tuning needed to serve the model well — so picking a template is the only knob you turn for "how do I want this model to run.".

qwen3-32b, for example, ships with four templates the deploy wizard exposes side by side:.

It has been revealed that each template arrives pre-tuned for the model — runtime settings, tool-call and reasoning parsers, scoring path, health probes, request concurrency, and any model-specific context-extension settings are all set by Microsoft, with any trade-offs called out inline in the template description. When you script the deploy, you reference the template and Foundry handles the rest.

The deployment is reachable through the unified Foundry endpoint with the OpenAI SDK — the `model` field takes the deployment name you just created:.

A chat-completions model from the Collection slots into Foundry Agents as an admin-connected model and is callable through the Foundry Responses API with the same OpenAI SDK — same auth, same endpoint, same observability.

Available now in preview: the Hugging Face Collection in the Microsoft Foundry Model Catalog — thousands of models across every modality, refreshed weekly, deployable onto Foundry Managed Compute with NVIDIA A100, NVIDIA H100, or AMD MI300X accelerators in Global and Data Zone scopes, behind a unified Foundry endpoint with Playground support, first-class Azure Monitor metrics, per-deployment billing tags, and curated runtime upgrades and CVE patching applied automatically to your deployments.

On the roadmap: broader coverage of the Hugging Face ecosystem, additional accelerator families, and Bring Your Own Weights for fine-tuned and proprietary variants deployed through the same templates and governance as Collection models.

According to recent reports, hugging Face is where open models are published and discovered. Microsoft Foundry is where enterprises operationalize them — on curated, license-screened, security-screened weights hosted in Azure; on community-built and CVE-scanned runtimes; behind a single endpoint with enterprise identity, networking, observability, and agent integration on top. The breadth of the open-source ecosystem, with the operational layer Microsoft runs underneath. For a deep dive on Foundry Managed Compute — pricing, accelerator SKUs, data residency, enterprise readiness, observability, and the full Responses API + memory pattern — see the Managed Compute launch blog.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft announced this week that its To Do app is shutting down soon, taking the legacy of Wunderlist with it.

Microsoft is shutting down its To Do app at the end of June 2027, with focus moving to the newer Planner app. The firm explains:.

As we bring personal task management into Planner, we will phase out To Do. The To Do apps will retire on June 30, 2027. Connections that other apps use to access To Do tasks will continue beyond that date, and we’ll provide separate notice before those connections are retired. We’re also updating existing task integrations across Microsoft 365 to connect with Planner, so you’ll be able to create or manage tasks in the Microsoft experiences you already use. Although To Do tasks are already visible in Planner, they will not be migrated to the new private plan. Customers using personal Microsoft accounts will need to choose another app. Our To Do transition guidance  will help you understand what’s changing and plan your next steps.

According to recent reports, to Do was built on the foundation of Wunderlist, a wildly popular to do list app that Microsoft purchased in 2015. Wunderlist later shut down in 2020.

According to recent reports, microsoft’s shuffle, notably, leaves general consumers without a replacement app. To Do was available to anyone with a Microsoft account, where Planner is available only to enterprise/business people. So, for long-time Wunderlist users who followed Microsoft migration, this is the end of the road and it’s officially time to move to another app.

So the cost of the overall device is more influenced by memory prices than in a flagship, like the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Even with a specced-out build, there’s more dispersion of costly components, rather than one expensive component like memory taking up the bulk of the production price.

That cut is estimated to be around 10 million units, and this latest report only furthers the claim that mid-range devices are too costly to make for Samsung.

The opposite is true for the Galaxy S27 Pro and Ultra, which reportedly got the green light for increased production prior to launch. Price suggestions average an increase of $200 for the Galaxy S27 and Galaxy S27 Plus. As for the high-spec Galaxy S27 Pro and Ultra, they start at $1,399 and $1,499, respectively.

From Hugging Face to Amazon SageMaker Studio in one click

📅 07 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (826 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, we’re excited to announce a deep-link integration between Hugging Face and Amazon SageMaker AI.
  • Recent findings suggest that previously, getting started on SageMaker Studio after discovering a model on Hugging Face required navigating multiple steps between opening Amazon SageMaker AI in the AWS Console, creating a domain, configuring IAM permissions, and sometimes requesting GPU quota.
  • “At Arcee, we build open models so developers and enterprises can actually own what they run: inspect the weights, post-train on their own data, and deploy on their own terms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we’re excited to announce a deep-link integration between Hugging Face and Amazon SageMaker AI. Developers can now go from model discovery to hands-on experimentation in SageMaker Studio with a single selection. Whether you fine-tune a foundation model (FM) from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart or deploy it to an Amazon SageMaker Inference endpoint, you can now land directly inside the relevant SageMaker Studio workflow. Your selected model is pre-loaded, and the environment is fully configured and ready to go.

Recent findings suggest that previously, getting started on SageMaker Studio after discovering a model on Hugging Face required navigating multiple steps between opening Amazon SageMaker AI in the AWS Console, creating a domain, configuring IAM permissions, and sometimes requesting GPU quota. For developers who want to iterate rapidly, this friction slows down the path from inspiration to experimentation. The integration creates a more direct path from discovery to enterprise deployment.

“At Arcee, we build open models so developers and enterprises can actually own what they run: inspect the weights, post-train on their own data, and deploy on their own terms. This integration takes that promise the last mile. Going from an open model on Hugging Face straight into SageMaker Studio in a single click, then fine-tuning or deploying it inside your own AWS environment with nothing to wire up, is the kind of experience open models have been missing. Open weights you own, running in the cloud you control. That is exactly the combination our customers have been asking for.”.

— Mark McQuade, Founder and CEO, Arcee AI.

With the launch of a one-click Studio landing experience, choosing Customize on SageMaker AI or Deploy on SageMaker AI on a supported Hugging Face model page takes you directly to the console. SageMaker AI then automatically provisions a newly introduced domain with pre-configured permissions in seconds and carries the model context through.

This launch introduces three capabilities that shorten the path from a Hugging Face model to a working SageMaker Studio workflow.

When you browse models on Hugging Face, you’ll now see action buttons alongside supported models that map directly to SageMaker Studio workflows:.

Each entry point preserves the context, meaning you don’t need to search for the model again once inside Studio.

New Studio environments created through this flow come with permissions already configured for the full range of SageMaker AI capabilities, including model customization, training jobs, notebook experimentation, and endpoint deployment. A new managed policy, AmazonSageMakerModelCustomizationCoreAccess, is created and attached for you. It provides permissions for serverless model customization jobs using supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF), with supported deployment to SageMaker AI or Amazon Bedrock endpoints. This alleviates the need to manually create and configure AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles and policies before you can start experimenting. For existing Studio environments, actionable messages with direct links to documentation guide you through adding these permissions.

Sources indicate that when selecting instance types for deployment or training, the Studio UI now surfaces quota availability directly in the instance selection list. You can immediately see which GPU instance types (G5, G6) are available under your account’s current limits. You don’t need to navigate separately to Service Quotas. If you still need to request a limit increase, you’re redirected directly to the Service Quotas page for the respective instance type.

Let’s walk through the experience of customizing or deploying a model starting from Hugging Face.

According to recent reports, on the Hugging Face model page, click on “Deploy” and select “Amazon SageMaker AI”. If the model is supported, you will see two buttons, “Deploy on SageMaker AI” and “Customize on SageMaker AI”. Then select “Customize on SageMaker AI” for a supported model.

You’re prompted to sign in to AWS using your existing credentials. If you already have an active console session, this step is skipped automatically. For more information, see Sign in to the AWS Management Console.

In a recent development, you arrive directly on the Model Customization page inside SageMaker Studio with your model pre-selected. Next, configure your fine-tuning parameters such as training data, hyperparameters, and instance type, then submit the customization job.

It has been revealed that alternatively, selecting Deploy on SageMaker AI opens the endpoint deployment page in Studio with the model pre-configured. Select your instance type (quota visibility included), review the settings, and deploy.

After you deploy your endpoint, test inference directly from Studio’s endpoint testing interface.

You can try this experience today:.

Industry observers note that the launch of a one-click Studio landing experience minimizes the friction between discovering a model and experimenting with it. By connecting Hugging Face directly to the SageMaker Studio workflows, developers can stay in their flow. There’s no context switching, no manual environment setup, and no permission troubleshooting.

To get started, visit the Amazon SageMaker Studio page or explore models on Hugging Face and choose Deploy or Customize on SageMaker AI.

Despite the fact that Moto Tag 2 has only been on the market for a few months at this point, Motorola is apparently getting Moto Tag 3 out in the not-too-distant future, and it’s already on sale (probably by mistake).

Industry observers note that an Amazon UK listing went up this week for “Moto Tag 3,” a newly introduced version of Motorola’s Android Find Hub tracker. The listing shows the tracker in “Pantone Lucent White,” while a second image shared by Evan Blass shows the new model in a vibrant purple color.

There’s no indication of major changes in “Moto Tag 3,” with Motorola still claiming similar battery life, using a CR2032 battery, and supporting UWB in Android Find Hub.

The listing (thanks Matt!) explains:.

Motorola moto tag 3 helps you locate everyday items with precision and reliability. Using Ultra Wideband and Bluetooth technology, it works with the Android Find Hub network to track belongings both nearby and at distance. With more than 500 days of battery life powered by a replaceable CR2032 battery, it is designed for long-term use. Built-in privacy protections, encrypted location data, and unwanted tracking alerts support secure tracking in a compact, IP68-rated design suitable for daily carry.

It has been revealed that “Moto Tag 3” is on sale from Amazon UK, though it comes with a “1-4 month” shipping estimate. This is almost certainly a slip-up, especially given the timing.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The transformers library has become the reference modeling library for Machine Learning.
  • According to recent reports, we have fully embraced this role in the ecosystem and are investing a lot of effort to make it easier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that TL;DR: The transformers vLLM backend is now as fast (or faster) than custom vLLM implementations for many LLM architectures. Model authors can automatically leverage their transformers implementations to get ultra fast vLLM inference, for free.

The transformers library has become the reference modeling library for Machine Learning. It supports 450+ architectures through consistent APIs, and is designed with the main goal that model implementations are self contained and easy to understand. Going through transformers code makes it easy for contributors to learn how an architecture works, and then port it to other frameworks such as vLLM, SGLang, MLX, llama.cpp, and many others.

According to recent reports, we have fully embraced this role in the ecosystem and are investing a lot of effort to make it easier. A substantial step in this direction was the integration last year of transformers as a modeling backend in vLLM. This has been allowing model authors to run transformers models (LLMs and VLMs alike) inside vLLM, without having to port anything. Transformers provides the modeling code, and vLLM provides extremely optimized inference techniques such as continuous batching and custom attention kernels.

This integration gets better now 🚀!

We put the transformers modeling backend for vLLM head to head with vLLM's hand written native implementations across three very different Qwen3 models:.

Recent findings suggest that running any* Hugging Face model through the transformers modeling backend is a single flag — --model-impl transformers. It composes with the usual parallelism options, so nothing about your serving setup changes:.

*Models that use linear attention are not at the moment supported, but they will be soon! Custom models where the code lives in a Hub repo are unlikely to work as they will not have been written compliantly.

Each model is compared under three conditions that are identical in every way except the code path:.

The full, reproducible runner is available as a gist: benchmark.sh.

Recent findings suggest that the transformers modeling backend for vLLM used to focus on attention as the bottleneck for inference. By plugging vLLM’s attention implementation at runtime, we could make a transformers model run efficiently inside the vLLM engine. But there are many dimensions to deployments that only a custom port can target to extract maximum inference performance. Parallelization across GPUs, compilation, fused kernels, and many more, all contribute to leveraging your hardware to achieve ultra-fast inference.

When model authors wanted the absolute best performance, they were still writing custom vLLM implementations.

The latest iteration of the transformers modeling backend for vLLM dynamically applies inference specific layer fusions at runtime to match the speed of custom code implementations, for compatible architectures.

The transformers modeling backend for vLLM now uses torch.fx to perform static analysis on the model’s graph. This process searches for known patterns that can be optimised. After any patterns have been identified, it uses ast (abstract syntax tree) to manipulate the source code and rewrite some of the operations in place.

As shown above, this results in native vLLM inference speed for compatible models, without having to write a single line of code to optimize the model for inference.

We are in the process of writing a detailed blog post to dive deep inside these optimized inference methods and explain in detail how we manipulate the model to adapt to them.

One provenance implication here is that the model definition and the executed inference graph are no longer the same artifact boundary.

If the runtime rewrites model code and replaces modules with fused kernels, deployment evidence probably needs to preserve both the source model identity and the transformation/runtime path.

5 Things Most Developers Get Wrong When Turning Images into HTML

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • According to recent reports, weekly.
  • Turning a design image into a working webpage can look simple.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

According to recent reports, weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Turning a design image into a working webpage can look simple.

You have a picture (a mockup, a screenshot, a Figma export), and your job is to turn it into working HTML in a browser.

But here is the catch. A design image is static, while a webpage is dynamic and responsive across different screen sizes and devices. A webpage needs to load promptly, adapt perfectly to different screen sizes, and allow touch interactions on mobile devices.

Most mistakes in this process happen when the conversion is treated as copying a picture instead of rebuilding it.

This section walks you through the mistakes developers often make, and more importantly, how to fix each of them.

In a recent development, whether you are slicing a client mockup or converting a screenshot into code, avoiding these mistakes can save you from hours of rework. Let’s get into the details.

A screenshot reflects how a page appears at a particular display. But it doesn’t show how the layout will behave when the content changes or the screen gets smaller.

It has been revealed that developers sometimes try to copy the exact positions and dimensions of every element. To match the screenshot, they may use fixed widths, large margins, and absolute positioning.

This can work at one screen size, but the layout may break on smaller screens or when a heading wraps onto an extra line.

The better approach is identifying the layout rules behind the design. CSS Grid can arrange the cards in columns. Flexbox can help align elements within each card. And media queries can adjust the layout for smaller screens.

Pixel-level comparison can be useful in some cases, but it should not come at the cost of a flexible layout.

Industry observers note that when developers recreate a design, it’s easier for them to focus on shapes and spacing rather than the purpose of each element. So, they may use generic elements for headings, buttons, navigation areas, and content sections instead of choosing elements that reflect each element's purpose.

This may produce the right appearance, but it often makes the code harder to maintain and understand. And when developers fail to use the right HTML elements, it can also create accessibility problems later.

It has been revealed that so don’t put everything inside several unnamed containers. Instead, use a clear structure with appropriate headings, meaningful alt text for informative images, and real buttons for actions.

Semantic elements (e.g., header, nav, main, section, and footer) can also help organize a large page when they match the content’s purpose.

A design image may have headings, descriptions, prices, labels, or button text.

Reusing the entire image to reproduce the original design feels quick. But it can create problems when that text has to work as part of a responsive web page.

According to recent reports, for example, there’s a promotional banner that contains a heading, a short description, and a CTA button. If you use the entire banner as one image, you can’t easily change the heading, translate the text, or make the button work as a real element.

Sources indicate that so, don’t treat the image like that. Instead, use the original image where appropriate and recreate the text and button in HTML. CSS can control their position, size, color, and spacing.

Make sure you distinguish between visual elements that should remain images and text that should be recreated as HTML.

Not every part of turning images into HTML needs to be done manually.

Industry observers note that developers sometimes spend too much time on recreating basic elements when there are free online conversion tools available. These tools can help them get an initial version much faster.

An online conversion tool may be helpful when you need to extract text or generate a rough starting layout from a design image.

For example, you can upload a design image into an online image to html converter to get a starting point (rather than starting from a blank file). Review the tool’s output. Identify the parts you can reuse (as they are) and tweak the parts that need adjustments.

Keep in mind that the first result generated by the tool isn’t the final code. You may need to reorganize the HTML, refine the CSS, and adjust the layout to make it responsive.

Use automation where it saves time and your own judgement where it matters.

A screenshot demonstrates just one view of a page. It doesn’t show how the layout may change on a phone or how people using a keyboard/screen reader can interact with it.

So, developers who focus only on the desktop design may end up with:.

buttons that are difficult to use.

content that becomes too small on mobile devices.

There’s also a chance of accessibility problems when images lack suitable alt text/interactive elements.

In a recent development, let’s say a page has three cards in a row. On the desktop, this arrangement may work well. But on a phone, you may need to stack the cards vertically so their content remains readable.

Industry observers note that that’s why accessibility should be considered during the same process. Use meaningful headings and provide appropriate alt text for images. Also, maintain sufficient text contrast and make sure interactive elements can be operated with a keyboard.

Lastly, don’t forget to test the page on both desktop and mobile screen sizes before finalizing it.

HTML and CSS handle the structure and appearance of a webpage, but JavaScript makes it possible to add interactive features.

For example, a design image may contain a navigation menu with a button. When recreating this design, developers should make sure the button performs an actual action rather than simply looking like a clickable element.

You can use JavaScript's event listeners to handle these interactions.

Now, add JavaScript to make the menu functional:.

In this example, clicking the button opens or closes the navigation menu. The aria-expanded attribute also communicates the menu's current state to assistive technologies.

According to recent reports, this is a simple example of why converting a design image into HTML involves more than matching its appearance. Developers also need to recreate the behavior of interactive elements using appropriate HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

The process of turning an image into HTML feels easy when you treat it the right way.

Recent findings suggest that start by identifying the main sections, text, images, and interactive elements. Then create meaningful HTML and build the layout with CSS. Make the necessary adjustments to ensure it works across different screen sizes.

Sources indicate that use a conversion tool when it can really save time. But don’t forget to review the generated output of the tool thoroughly before using it.

In a recent development, A screenshot is a visual reference, not a complete set of development instructions. And the best result for you isn’t simply a page that looks like the image.

It is a page that also works well, adapts well, and stays easy to maintain.

It’s got a 5ATM rating and a polycarbonate case, so it’s quite durable.

The Garmin Bounce 2 is preloaded with a few mini games and educational apps, plus the Garmin Jr. app has built-in unlockables and rewards parents can set for doing chores, completing schoolwork, etc. Battery life is roughly 2 days with normal use, but can be less if you’re in an area with poor LTE reception. The Bark Watch uses Samsung Galaxy Watch 8 hardware and a custom version of Wear OS. It’s a much more powerful watch and only gets a day of battery life because of it. It doesn’t have any games, social media, or browsers.

Since it uses Samsung’s hardware, it includes cutting-edge health sensors that your kids can use, plus great multitasking and a svelte, attractive design. Bark charges $15 per month for its strategy, which includes a Bark App subscription for the whole family. I also use the Bark App on my son’s phone, which helps me monitor his usage and make sure he’s safe online. The extra $5 per month adds up, but it’s absolutely worth it if you want to add the Bark App to another phone or tablet.

The Bark Watch is fine enough for younger kids, but the design and lack of games feel more like an “older kids’ watch” to me, and my 12-year-old son agrees. Either way you go, these are fantastic choices that you’ll be happy with, especially with a nice little deal.
