OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, and Cursor are all sending webhooks now, and all four built them on Standard Webhooks, the open spec written by Svix. Downloads of the spec's npm package went from 1.7 million a month in September 2025 to 220 million a month currently.

Sources indicate that this may be boring to hear for the nth time, but the reason is agents. An individual person checks on a running job a few times. An agent told to watch for changes checks every resource, every minute, for as long as it runs, and almost every one of those requests comes back with nothing latest. An agent that starts a job, polls until it finishes, and then starts the next one spends most of its time waiting: six steps with 15 seconds of polling each add 90 seconds, even when every operation is fast. Polling more often adds load, and polling less often adds delay, so there's not really a sweet spot.

Sources indicate that an event-driven API gets rid of that trade-off. It tells consumers when something changed or finished, so they stop asking. That matters most for work that runs for minutes or hours, like batch inference, fine-tuning, and video generation, and many APIs still don't offer it. Of the 57 AI APIs with long-running jobs that Svix reviewed for its State of Webhooks 2027 report, 19 make you poll for the result.

Webhooks are how most APIs push those events, and you can get a v1 out pretty fast. Making it dependable is an infrastructure problem, which is a class of problem that requires more time by default. Before you ship webhooks, you need an append-only event log behind every delivery, a fixed event format, signed payloads, retries with backoff, event IDs receivers can deduplicate on, per-endpoint isolation, and delivery logs your customers can read. If you skip one of these things, a customer is just going to bring it up later.

Each section below covers one of them with adaptable code, and Standard Webhooks works with existing verification libraries in most languages.

If the request handler that changes the data also sends the webhook, a crash between the commit and the HTTP call loses the event, and nothing records that it should have gone out. A customer whose endpoint was down for longer than your retry window has no way to find out what they missed.

Both problems go away if you write each event to an append-only table, scoped per customer, in the same transaction as the change. Webhooks are delivered from that table, and the same table backs an HTTP endpoint customers can read from a cursor. Svix calls this design POKE (Publish Once, Kickoff Everywhere). Build the log first: a consumer who misses a webhook needs somewhere to resume from.

Every code path that changes state calls one helper inside its own transaction:.

Pass the helper the transaction handle. An insert through the connection pool commits separately, so you can end up with the event and no change, or the change and no event.

According to recent reports, the advisory lock prevents a subtler bug. Postgres assigns sequence values at insert time, but rows only become visible at commit. With two concurrent writers, a reader can see ID 102, store it as its cursor, and then never see ID 101 when the slower transaction commits. Holding a per-customer lock until commit makes each customer's events visible in ID order.

According to recent reports, reading the log is one indexed range query. The endpoint returns a cursor even when there are no latest events, so a client can always store it and ask again later:.

Industry observers note that authenticate stands in for the middleware that already protects your API and sets req.customerId. That scoping stops one customer from reading another's events. A customer who was offline for a week asks for events after their last cursor and gets everything they missed, in order. Publish your retention period, since it limits how far back that works. The same log can also serve synthetic created events for existing records when a new integration needs to load its initial state.

Customers write handlers against your payloads, so you'll be supporting every field you ship.

In a recent development, give each event an id, type, timestamp, and data. Use the log row's ID as the event ID so webhooks and the pull endpoint agree. Name types as a resource plus a past-tense action, like invoice.paid, and publish a catalog with an example payload for each type.

According to recent reports, emit an event for each state change a consumer would otherwise poll for. Deletions are the ones teams forget most. Long-running jobs need completion and failure events, such as export.completed and export.failed.

Adding a field is safe. Removing or renaming one breaks handlers, so ship a newly introduced type such as invoice.paid.v2 and keep sending the old one until customers have moved over.

Anyone who finds a customer's webhook URL can POST a fake invoice.paid to it. A signature lets the receiver confirm the request came from you, wasn't modified in transit, and isn't an old request being replayed.

Standard Webhooks signs the string id.timestamp.body with HMAC-SHA256, using a separate secret for each endpoint. Including the timestamp is what lets receivers reject old requests. Generate secrets with "whsec_" + crypto.randomBytes(24).toString("base64").

In a recent development, send the result in three headers. The ID comes from the log and stays the same on every retry. The timestamp is the time of the current attempt, so each retry gets a upcoming signature.

Receivers need the matching check, so put it in your docs:.

Industry observers note that the function takes the raw body because frameworks that parse JSON and serialize it again change the bytes, and the signature stops matching. It compares with crypto.timingSafeEqual, since === returns faster on an early mismatch and leaks timing information. It rejects requests more than five minutes old to block replays. The signature header is a space-separated list so that during a secret rotation you can send one signature per secret and the receiver accepts either.

Sources indicate that that code highlights how the scheme works. In production, use a Standard Webhooks library on both ends. It implements the same algorithm:.

Industry observers note that receiving endpoints go down during deploys and outages, and they return errors when they're rate limited. If you only try once, each of those is a lost webhook.

Industry observers note that count any non-2xx response as a failure, redirects included. Following a redirect to an arbitrary host is a security problem in its own right. Count slow responses as failures too. The code below gives up after 15 seconds. Publish whatever limit you pick, because customer handlers have to respond within it.

Recent findings suggest that these delays match the schedule Svix runs in production: eight attempts over a little more than 27 hours. The early retries cover restarts. The later ones give someone time to notice an outage and fix it. After each failure, pass the number of attempts so far to nextAttemptAt, and when it returns null, mark the delivery as failed. The event is still in the log, so once the customer fixes their server they can replay it or read it from the pull endpoint.

Store attempt state in a table next to the log. Timers in process memory disappear when the process restarts, and you don't need a message broker to avoid that.

Decide what happens to endpoints that never come back. Svix disables an endpoint after five days of continuous failure and emits an event so the sender can tell the customer. Pick your own threshold, notify the customer when you disable their endpoint, and let them turn it back on.

It has been revealed that retries mean some events arrive twice. Usually the receiver processed the event but timed out before you saw its response, so you sent it again. Senders accept this at-least-once behavior because the alternative is dropping events, and receivers handle the duplicates.

It has been revealed that receivers deduplicate on webhook-id, which doesn't change between retries. The insert that stores the event can also be the duplicate check:.

webhook_inbox needs a text primary key id and a jsonb column payload. The handler verifies the signature, stores the event, and returns 204. A background worker processes the inbox, so the handler responds well within the sender's timeout. express.raw gives the route the unparsed body that verification needs.

In a recent development, put this pattern in your docs with a note about ordering. Events in the log have a fixed order, but webhook deliveries don't always arrive in it. A retried invoice.created can land after invoice.paid. Receivers should keep whichever event has the newer updated_at, or read the pull endpoint when they need strict ordering.

With a shared worker pool, one customer's hanging endpoint can tie up every worker for the full timeout while other customers' events wait. Limit concurrent deliveries per endpoint, and slow down delivery to endpoints that keep failing.

Customer-supplied URLs are also an attack surface. Someone can register http://169.254.169.254/ or an internal hostname and get your servers to call your cloud metadata service or private network. This is server-side request forgery (SSRF). Resolve the hostname before connecting, reject private and loopback addresses, and don't follow redirects. The delivery code sets redirect: "manual" for this reason.

Without a self-serve view, every "did you send it?" question goes to an engineer who has to search logs.

Give customers a page to add and remove endpoints, choose event types, and rotate secrets. For each message, show every attempt with its timestamp, status code, and response body. The response body usually contains the customer's own error message. Add buttons to replay a failed message and to send a test event.

Sources indicate that expose the same operations in your API. Creating an endpoint and choosing its event types should take one authenticated request, because scripts and AI agents now set up a lot of integrations and can't click through a dashboard.

This is the biggest item here because it needs a UI, and it's the one teams most often leave out of the first release.

You can build all of this yourself, and many teams have. It comes down to the fact that it's cheap to manage delivery for 99% of your webhooks, but it's nontrivial to guarantee it for 100% of them. This is also ignoring the UX side such as offering the customer portal for your customers to manage their webhooks in.

Industry observers note that svix, which sponsored this article, handles webhook delivery. You keep the event log and decide what goes in it. A small relay reads fresh rows and passes each one to Svix:.

Industry observers note that svix also hosts the debugging portal. This call returns a single-use link where the customer can manage endpoints, read delivery logs, and replay messages:.

The free tier includes 50,000 messages a month and doesn't require a credit card.

Industry News: Record, train, and deploy from one place with Strands Agents, LeRobot, and Hugging Face Storage Buckets

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A walkthrough of the streaming data loop in Strands Robots, one loop that records robot demonstrations, trains on them by reading straight from the Hub, and deploys the policy back to hardware, with the dataset in the same on-disk LeRobot format the whole way through.
  • In a recent development, you have an agent that can already drive a robot while your code records a demonstration and pushes it to the Hugging Face Hub.
  • Industry observers note that the first post in this series introduced Strands Robots, an open source SDK from AWS (Apache 2.0) that exposes robot abstractions, simulation, and the LeRobot stack as AgentTools you compose into a single Strands agent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A walkthrough of the streaming data loop in Strands Robots, one loop that records robot demonstrations, trains on them by reading straight from the Hub, and deploys the policy back to hardware, with the dataset in the same on-disk LeRobot format the whole way through.

Updated for Strands Robots 0.6 and LeRobot 0.7.

In a recent development, you have an agent that can already drive a robot while your code records a demonstration and pushes it to the Hugging Face Hub. Now you want to run that loop continuously: collect episodes through the day, train a policy on the growing dataset, deploy it, and pull the next batch back to improve it. Run that loop once and every piece works. Run it every day and you start paying for the same byte transfers over and over. The recordings you upload keep growing, each training run copies the whole dataset to the GPUs before it starts, and every newly introduced checkpoint ships out while the next batch of recordings comes back.

Industry observers note that the first post in this series introduced Strands Robots, an open source SDK from AWS (Apache 2.0) that exposes robot abstractions, simulation, and the LeRobot stack as AgentTools you compose into a single Strands agent. That post followed the agent loop in one direction, from a Hub dataset to a physical robot. This one follows the data the other way, from the first recorded frame back to the deployed policy, over Hugging Face Storage Buckets - a mutable, non-versioned, Xet-backed object-storage repository type announced in March 2026. A bucket sits beside your dataset repositories in the same hf:// namespace and uses the hf CLI you already have, so it becomes the working layer that holds your data between the day you record it and the day you train on it.

Sources indicate that someone has to decide which episodes to keep, when the scene has drifted far enough to re-record, whether today's batch is enough to train on, and which checkpoint replaces the one on the arm. Each of those decisions comes up dozens of times over a collection campaign, and each one needs a look at what came back before the next command goes out. That is the work an agent is for: it drives the robot and reads the results, while the recording itself stays one line of your code. This post walks you through the data loop: record a demonstration into a Storage Bucket, store it so that each sync uploads only the bytes that changed, train by streaming the dataset straight from the Hub instead of downloading it, and deploy the checkpoint back to hardware with one keyword argument change. The runnable companion to this post lives at notebooks/12_streaming_data_loop.ipynb.

Sources indicate that where the first post recorded a dataset and pushed it to the Hub, the loop you build here records a LeRobotDataset with one run(record=...) call, syncs it into a Storage Bucket, and streams that same dataset back frame by frame, decoding camera video on the fly, with no local copy. You read it back with LeRobot's own streaming reader, so the dataset Robot() recorded is exactly the one LeRobot trains on. Your trained checkpoint then deploys to that same Robot() with one keyword argument change, and the demonstrations it records on hardware return to the same bucket.

Figure 1. The four stages share one backend. Robot("so101") records a LeRobotDataset with run(record=...); hf sync syncs it into a Storage Bucket; lerobot-train reads it back over the Hub through LeRobot's StreamingLeRobotDataset with no full download; and the trained checkpoint deploys to the same Robot with a port=. The on-disk format stays exactly as LeRobot wrote it.

When the agent runs an episode, it invokes one tool, and the rollout then proceeds at the robot's control frequency until the episode ends, with the policy producing every action. Stripped down to the code, the whole loop is a handful of lines:.

What follows is what's actually happening inside that loop, step by step.

That's it. Every stage in this post runs on a laptop with these three, plus the bucket and training items under Advanced. What runs is the loop, not a working policy: the default path uses a placeholder wave function, which records a valid dataset but not a useful one.

Sources indicate that you record new episodes through the day, each a continuous run of camera frames and joint state-action telemetry. LeRobot writes that as a small set of large files that grow as you record. Push them into a versioned dataset repository and every append becomes a commit, and every revision is retained. Collection wants the reverse: somewhere to write bytes and overwrite them in place. That is a Storage Bucket, which lives inside your Hugging Face workspace and uses the permissions you already have. There are no identity and access management (IAM) roles to configure, no cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) rules, and no upload service to maintain.

Industry observers note that strands Robots records a LeRobotDataset in the same format LeRobot writes on hardware: pass record= to run(), and each run adds one episode. Record the episodes, then sync the finished dataset into a bucket. The wave function is a placeholder that produces joint targets without a trained model, so you can run the whole loop before you have a checkpoint to run:.

The sync writes to hf://buckets/{bucket}/{run_id}, where run_id is the folder name that follows the bucket, cube_pick here. The streaming read in Step 3 names the run too: the first two segments of the id are the bucket, and everything after them is the path inside it.

It has been revealed that each sync uploads only the files that changed. Write to the bucket through the day, and publish a versioned copy to a dataset repository when you want one: record="hf://my_user/cube_picking", push=True does that at the end of a run. The placeholder episodes are not useful training data. Pass a trained Policy("") to run() instead.

To record on a physical SO-101, LeRobot's record CLI handles the leader-follower bring-up:.

The dataset lands on disk in the same format as the simulation recording, so the same sync takes it to a bucket: hf sync ~/.cache/huggingface/lerobot/my_user/cube_picking hf://buckets/my-org/robot-fave/run-021. Collection runs append into one place, and your published repositories only get the versions you choose to publish.

Now that a dataset is in the bucket, the question is what the next sync costs you. Point two fixed cameras at an arm clearing the same table for eight hours and most of what you record is pixels you already have: the same lighting, the same chassis, the same background, across thousands of episodes. On a versioned repository it gets worse, because changing one frame in a multi-gigabyte video shard re-uploads the whole file.

Buckets are backed by Xet, which deduplicates your uploads at the byte level using content-defined chunking. Chunk boundaries follow the content, so inserting a few bytes changes only the chunk it lands in instead of shifting every boundary after it. In Hugging Face's own measurements (HF Storage), content-defined chunking reduces data transferred per upload by about four times across the Hub, and on Enterprise prepares billing is on the deduplicated footprint. Their bucket benchmarks show what that looks like on a single file. Starting from a 500 MB upload, changing 1% of the bytes and re-uploading moved 5.5 MB, changing 5% moved 27.5 MB, and changing 10% moved 55 MB. Without chunk-level deduplication, overwriting an object means sending all of its bytes again, whether or not they changed.

How much that saves you depends on the file layout, and the Strands Robots recorder uses LeRobot's. Episodes go into Parquet shards (data/chunk-000/file-000.parquet) and per-camera MP4 shards (videos/observation.images.front/chunk-000/file-000.mp4), rolling to a newly introduced file when the current one fills, at LeRobot's defaults of 100 MB for data Parquet and 200 MB for video MP4. Each run(record=...) starts its own shards, and a lerobot-record session grows its open shard until it fills. Either way, a sync after a day of recording uploads the new trailing shards plus, at most, the one partially-filled shard that grew, rather than the whole dataset. Sync the same bucket again tomorrow and Xet handles the deduplication.

It has been revealed that figure 2. A sync uploads only what changed. The first sync of a fresh dataset uploads every chunk; after recording more episodes, Xet's content-defined chunking means the next sync uploads only the fresh chunks and skips the ones already stored.

To train, you point GPUs at your dataset. Download it first and those GPUs sit idle until hundreds of gigabytes finish copying. Streaming straight from the Hub works here because of the shard layout from Step 2: a batch becomes a few byte-range reads over large shards rather than thousands of small fetches. LeRobot's StreamingLeRobotDataset turns that into a drop-in torch iterable, and it opens a bucket with repo_type="bucket":.

Recent findings suggest that figure 3. Stream, don't download. The download path copies the whole dataset to local disk first, so the GPU waits; StreamingLeRobotDataset reads batches straight from the bucket with only metadata on local disk, so the GPU trains from the first batch.

Recent findings suggest that nothing lands on local disk except the small meta/ folder of schema, statistics, and episode index, plus a seek index for the video shards: a full streaming read of the 86 MB lerobot/svla_so101_pickplace dataset left under 1 MB on disk. Camera frames are decoded from the remote MP4 shards as you iterate; state and action come from the Parquet shards. That loop reads one frame at a time, which suits inspecting an episode. To train, pass the reader to a DataLoader and iterate batches instead. The streaming dataset shuffles internally through a bounded reservoir buffer, so video decoding parallelizes across worker processes:.

On macOS, run that from a script with an if __name__ == "__main__": guard, because DataLoader workers start by re-importing the script.

It has been revealed that if you would rather not write the loop at all, LeRobot's own trainer reads through the same engine, so the dataset you collected trains without a line of new code. It takes a bucket through the same keyword argument the in-process reader uses:.

Sources indicate that buckets are streaming-only, so --dataset.repo_type=bucket requires --dataset.streaming=true and the config rejects the combination otherwise. --policy.push_to_hub=false keeps the checkpoint local; name a --policy.repo_id to publish it instead. Reach for StreamingLeRobotDataset directly when you want the loop in your own process: validating an episode, replaying it in simulation, or feeding a custom evaluation loop.

The checkpoint lerobot-train writes loads straight back through the same entry point used to run any other policy, so the record-train-deploy loop closes in a few lines:.

Recent findings suggest that A 20-step CPU run of ACT over the two-episode dataset above, streamed from a private bucket, wrote a checkpoint that Policy() loaded and ran on the simulated arm. Twenty steps over placeholder episodes check that the loop connects; it does not train a policy that grasps. Training time scales with dataset size, batch size, and step count, and a useful ACT policy needs real demonstrations and a GPU.

Hugging Face's pre-warming caches bucket data at edge locations near the cloud and region where your jobs run, so your cluster reads locally and the dataloader stays ahead of the GPU. In Hugging Face's own bucket benchmarks, a warm content delivery network (CDN) read hit about 1,086 MB/s on a 10 GB payload against 780 MB/s cold, and roughly 1,124 MB/s warm at 100 GB, measured on an m5dn.24xlarge in us-east-1. The full comparison against plain object storage, upload as well as download, is on that dashboard. Choosing where that data lives is a Storage Regions setting on Team and Enterprise aims, as of this writing US and EU, with Asia-Pacific and Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) regions confirmed as coming; outside those plans repositories are stored in the US.

In this step you take the checkpoint you just trained, run it on a physical robot, and record the next round of demonstrations with it. This is the same agent code from the first post. The keyword argument that changes is port=, which selects the physical arm; id= names its LeRobot calibration, cameras= names the image keys the policy was trained on, and operator= approves its moves.

Nothing moves on the real arm until operator= approves it. The demonstrations it records with record= are in the same LeRobot format you started with, ready to sync back to the bucket for the next training run.

If your data already lives on Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), nothing in this post changes: a LeRobotDataset is a directory of Parquet and MP4 shards, and every step reads it wherever it sits. A bucket adds the Hub-native path, the sync and the streaming read, with no storage to provision first.

Run the loop again tomorrow and you record into the same bucket, sync only what changed, and stream it to the GPUs without waiting for a download. The data never leaves the LeRobot format.

According to recent reports, the full Strands Robots sample is on GitHub at strands-labs/robots in notebooks/12_streaming_data_loop.ipynb. It walks you through the full loop cell by cell: record, sync to a bucket, stream back, train, and load the checkpoint. Every cell runs in simulation on the placeholder policy, so no GPU and no Docker are needed, and without a bucket set it needs no Hugging Face credentials either.

Run the cells top to bottom. To sync to a bucket, set HF_BUCKET=my-org/robot-fave before starting Jupyter (after hf auth login); each run syncs under its own folder, nb12-, and the notebook streams back from it. Without HF_BUCKET it trains from the local folder instead. To train on a GPU, raise --steps and drop --policy.device=cpu in the training cell.

Sources indicate that the snippets here are a "hello world" of the Strands Robots data loop. Five things change once you run it against real data.

According to recent reports, prompt injection. Supplying untrusted data to an agent can lead to prompt injection, where untrustworthy context is treated as LLM instructions. These agents actuate robots, so this is an important risk to track. Feed the agent only data from trusted sources. If not all input can be trusted, restrict the tools available to the agent so it cannot take safety-critical actions. In Strands Robots an agent cannot record, push, or calibrate, and on a real robot operator= answers every move and every policy run's initiative before anything moves.

Training data is a trust boundary. Anything that can write into the collection bucket can also write episodes that a policy later trains on, and that policy drives a physical arm. Keep the credential that writes collection data separate from the one a training job reads with, sync each run under its own run_id so an episode can be traced to the run that produced it and removed on its own, and treat the versioned dataset repository as the reviewed artifact, because the bucket keeps no revisions to audit against.

Industry observers note that bucket credentials and scope. hf sync and StreamingLeRobotDataset use the token from hf auth login. Use a token scoped to the specific namespace you are writing to, prefer --private buckets for collection data, and keep the bucket distinct from the versioned dataset repository you publish and share.

Industry observers note that overwrite in place keeps no revisions. A bucket overwrites in place and retains no revisions, which is what makes it a working layer and also means a repeated run_id replaces the run already stored there. Sync each collection run to its own path, as in hf sync ./recordings hf://buckets/my-org/robot-fave/run-021. For anything you need to be able to return to, push to a versioned dataset repository, where every revision is retained.

Sources indicate that only use trusted Hugging Face orgs. Loading a checkpoint runs code its publisher chose. A Policy your own code builds loads directly; a Hub checkpoint the agent asks for by name loads only if the operator lists it in STRANDS_POLICY_REPOS (for example STRANDS_POLICY_REPOS=lerobot/smolvla_base,my_user/*). Only load checkpoints from organizations you trust. Model weights can contain arbitrary code (pickle-based checkpoints). Prefer safetensors-format checkpoints where available.

Industry observers note that the loop leaves a bucket, datasets under /tmp, and a checkpoint on disk. Bucket contents count toward your stored volume, so remove what you no longer need:.

Stop any training process still on a GPU instance, and stop the instance. If you ran the notebook, its last cell prints the command that removes its run. Anything you published to a dataset repository is versioned and is untouched.

The Strands Robots documentation covers the robot catalog, simulation, policies, recording, and the mesh in depth. The recording guide documents run(record=...) and reading a dataset back with LeRobot.

Sources indicate that if you collect from more than one robot, give each one its own run_id and they write into the same bucket in parallel. The multi-robot mesh fans one agent out across those robots, so the same loop becomes a fleet collecting through the day into shared storage. A streaming reader reads one run at a time, so point each training run at the run_id it should learn from.

Industry observers note that if you want a larger policy than ACT, lerobot-train fine-tunes LeRobot's vision-language-action (VLA) policies, such as SmolVLA and pi0, on the dataset you just streamed, and the checkpoint loads as a Policy the same way. For heavier simulation to generate that data, the Newton (newton) and Isaac Sim (isaac) backends sit behind the same Robot(), so the agent code does not change as you scale up.

In a recent development, bucket streaming reached LeRobot through contributions from both the Strands Robots and LeRobot teams, upstream in LeRobot itself, so the datasets your agent collects are readable by every tool in that ecosystem. That runs both ways: the reader in Step 3 opens any of the LeRobot datasets already published on the Hub, so you can replay and evaluate against existing demonstrations before you record any of your own.

Recent findings suggest that contributions are welcome under Apache 2.0. If you build something with this loop, open an concern with what worked and what didn't.

What makes this architecture particularly compelling is that the agent isn’t just executing a task—it’s sitting inside a continuous data, learning, and deployment loop. Connecting data collection, streaming, training, evaluation, and deployment through one agent workflow opens up some fascinating possibilities for adaptive systems. At the same time, the trust boundaries around data, credentials, and agent actions become critical. This is where custom AI agent development and enterprise AI agent solutions need to be designed as complete systems rather than isolated agent features. Chinese web giant Tencent indicates new US GPU ban ‘sets everyone back in China’

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Don’t hoist the Mission Accomplished banner, because tech giant president thinks it also will spur China’s chip biz into action.
  • The USA’s upcoming ban on Chinese companies remotely accessing GPUs will have short-term impact, but ultimately see China accelerate its development of domestic alternatives, according to Martin Lau, the president of Chinese web giant Tencent.
  • Speaking on the manufacturer’s Q3 earnings call, Lau stated the new US regulation will have an “unfortunate” impact on Tencent’s business.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Don’t hoist the Mission Accomplished banner, because tech giant president thinks it also will spur China’s chip biz into action.

The USA’s upcoming ban on Chinese companies remotely accessing GPUs will have short-term impact, but ultimately see China accelerate its development of domestic alternatives, according to Martin Lau, the president of Chinese web giant Tencent.

Speaking on the manufacturer’s Q3 earnings call, Lau stated the new US regulation will have an “unfortunate” impact on Tencent’s business.

Industry observers note that “It does set everyone back. It sets everyone back in China,” Lau said. “So everyone is actually having less advanced compute to work with, no matter when you actually started leasing or building capacities outside of China.”.

He noted the ban will impact Tencent’s ability to train models.

“Our training efficiency with Hy4 is actually very high,” he mentioned. “When we look at the next version, it would take probably longer time for us to come up with the next version in the short run.”.

“But over time, the domestic supply chain would actually come on board.”.

Lau also thinks the bans won’t hamper Tencent’s ability to run inferencing workloads, because made-in-China chips “should be able to cover it.”.

Recent findings suggest that “And over the longer run, we believe all Chinese players would actually have to rely on domestic supply chains and domestic chips, which we see the industry is progressing very fast,” he added. “With the latest restriction, we expect it to actually speed up even further, because all the development effort would actually have to be focused on speeding up the domestic supply chain.”.

In a recent development, tencent needs GPUs, and lots of them, because the 10 million owners of its agentic assistant WorkBuddy are collectively consuming over 100 trillion tokens per day. Lau thinks WorkBuddy is on track to becoming a hit product, partly because many users are outside China.

Lau mentioned Tencent can serve WorkBuddy customers outside China because the service can operate with different models, and the firm thinks it can find third parties to provide the necessary inferencing services without the new US bans creating a problem.

But Lau said that GPU rentals and other cloud services, which are also growing strongly, may be impacted.

“In terms of cloud, if it is non-GPU related, we can actually build capacities ourselves outside of China,” he stated. “I think there is still a lot of such opportunities because our cloud service is actually very cost competitive. When it comes to GPU, then unfortunately, we cannot actually offer high-end GPU anymore. We may be able to work with some partners in different places.”.

Recent findings suggest that tencent doesn’t break out revenue for its cloud services, but noted they rose by 35 percent year-on-year, well ahead of the manufacturer’s overall eight percent growth. Marketing services also grew strongly, by 19 percent, thanks in part to fresh AI-powered systems that improve ad targeting.

The company’s WeChat and Weixin messaging platforms continued to grow, adding 35 million accounts to exiting the quarter with 1.44 billion monthly active customers.

One Tencent biz that went backwards was its international gaming unit, which saw revenue fall nine percent.

According to recent reports, chief strategy officer James Mitchell remarked that slowdown wasn’t caused by the release of Grand Theft Auto VI. “I think that in fairness, the slowdown for us predated the run-up to GTA VI,” he said, before predicting that Tencent’s existing and future “evergreen games” should help to turn things around.

According to recent reports, “The game environment globally is one where the rate of innovation has slowed somewhat, and now with AI, there’s opportunities to re-accelerate innovation,” he noted. ®.

State of Open Models: Summer 2026 Observations

📅 14 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2747 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in the AI world, time feels compressed.
  • Models and datasets on HF hub are growing on a daily basis.
  • Recent findings suggest that there used to be a clear progression path: labs would start by releasing smaller models and gradually work their way toward the top end of the scale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in the AI world, time feels compressed. A few months after our spring report in our biannual analysis worked through the ecosystem, there are quite a few findings that we have observed until this summer. This report lays out these observations from January to August 2026 and presents the data behind each one.

Models and datasets on HF hub are growing on a daily basis. Public model repositories grew from 2.43 to 2.96 million over the period, datasets from 711,000 to 1 million, Spaces from 1.00 to 1.44 million. The distribution underneath stays extreme, roughly 85.6% of models have fewer than 200 lifetime downloads, and 1.5% of repositories account for 99.2% of all downloads. Everything below happens inside that shape.

Recent findings suggest that there used to be a clear progression path: labs would start by releasing smaller models and gradually work their way toward the top end of the scale. In 2026, several Chinese labs skipped this progression entirely.

Industry observers note that in almost every month of 2026, the largest and most performant open model from a Chinese lab was larger than any model an American lab released. China's monthly ceiling ran between 754B and 2.78 trillion parameters; U.S. models stayed under 130B in five of seven months, the exception being NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 Ultra at 561B in May and June, and Inkling from Thinking Machines Lab.

Recent findings suggest that the chart splits the labs into two camps. Moonshot, MiniMax, Xiaomi and Z.ai publish almost nothing below 70B, so a developer's first encounter with them is a model too large to run on anything they own. Tencent and Alibaba Qwen cover the whole range instead, from under 1B upward.

Two things made the first camp possible. Building large stopped being a differentiator. Xiaomi, Ant Group and Meituan all cleared a trillion parameters this year, and neither was a household name in open weights twelve months ago. And a lab no longer has to ship a small model to be reachable, because the community's quantization layer will make a large one runnable within days, a dependency we return to below.

That leaves the size profile as a statement of intent rather than of capability. A frontier only portfolio stakes everything on benchmark position and API demand. A full spectrum portfolio is a bid to be the family developers standardise on. Both are rational, they are playing for different prizes.

The United States is not absent from open source.

The two organizations publishing the most new open models this year are also the companies making the hardware: AMD and NVIDIA. Each released more than 200 new model repositories, far ahead of the rest of the field, with LiquidAI ranking third at around 100. Hardware vendors have realized that open models are a way to sell chips: a model optimized for your hardware and freely available is the clearest proof that the hardware works.

Recent findings suggest that when smaller models and embedding models are included, where Google, Microsoft, IBM Granite, and OpenAI’s older vision and speech models generate hundreds of millions of downloads annually, U.S. open source AI is growing.

In a recent development, more hardware and infrastructure organizations such as NVIDIA are training and open-weighting competitive models. NVIDIA's Nemotron model family boasts high performance. Long-time leaders such as Meta reignite open roots with Meta's Muse Glimmer.

Sources indicate that at the frontier scale, some U.S. model releases above 100B parameters this year are built on top of Chinese models or leverage artifacts from Chinese labs, such as Thinking Machines’ Inkling (952B). Major original American models include NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3 Ultra (561B), Nemotron 3 Super (124B), and Arcee AI’s Trinity-Large (399B).

AMD contributed many conversions. This work is important: it enables trillion-parameter models to run efficiently on U.S. hardware. This represents a distribution and optimization layer.

Meanwhile, Chinese open models are increasingly optimized for domestic chips in China, the same competition in reverse, where models are designed around specific hardware ecosystems.

Industry observers note that we took the top 25 model repositories by downloads accumulated this year and the top 25 by likes. Exactly one repository appears in both lists.

Industry observers note that we counted downloads inside the window rather than lifetime, so nothing is credited for merely having existed longer, and controlling for age makes the split sharper. Not one model published in 2026 reaches the download top 25, while thirteen of the twenty-five date from 2022. all-MiniLM-L6-v2 was pulled 1.55 billion times in seven months against 5,156 likes; Kimi-K3 was pulled about 60 times per like it received.

The two numbers record different acts. A like states a release matters, and goes to frontier models in the weeks after they ship. A download says something is wired into a pipeline that runs on a schedule, and accrues to small, stable models over years. Likes are the right instrument for reading what the field is excited about, downloads for reading what it currently depends on. Treating either as a proxy for the other is the most common mistake we see in coverage of the Hub, including our own earlier work. The same split appears at the level of the publisher.

China's frontier labs are the only accounts on the Hub where the heavy band carries the volume. Effectively all of MiniMax's 2026 downloads are of models above 70B, along with 88% of Moonshot's, 55% of DeepSeek's and 39% of Z.ai's. No large American account looks like this: Google, Microsoft and IBM Granite record essentially none of their 2026 downloads above 70B, and NVIDIA and Meta only 14% and 9%.

Sources indicate that the difference becomes clearer in total downloads. Moonshot’s frontier-only portfolio recorded 37M downloads over the year, while Qwen’s broader release strategy across model sizes reached 2,045M (across repositories with declared parameter counts, 2,061M including all repositories) , about 55 times more. The continued expansion of the family, from the 2.4T-parameter Qwen 3.8 Max to smaller variants such as 27B, shows the same focus on coverage across different use cases.

Time also plays an vital role. Most models experience a sharp decline in usage after release, followed by a long tail of steady activity. A model’s adoption is largely determined within its first few months.

This helps explain why today’s download volume is often driven not by the newest releases, but by a smaller group of models that have become established infrastructure over time.

Sources indicate that if frontier models were a licensing business, you would expect the biggest releases to carry the tightest terms. However, the data below shows a different story.

Recent findings suggest that of 178 Chinese releases above 20B parameters this year, 59% carry Apache 2.0 and 22% carry MIT, and almost none carry non-commercial restrictions. However, in the last few weeks, we started to see a change on this trend for the really large models, with Kimi K3 and Qwen 3.8 2.4T starting to include some non-commercial restrictions and revenue share requirements to their licenses.

DeepSeek and Z.ai ship models between 700 billion and 1.65 trillion parameters under plain MIT. Chinese labs license their largest models about as permissively as their smallest, and more permissively than American labs license theirs: on the American side of the same size band, 29% is Apache or MIT, 41% sits under custom terms and 30% declares nothing at all.

Whatever these releases are for, it is not licence revenue. The weights are given away on the most permissive terms available. The return has to come from somewhere else: API and cloud business, hardware and platform positioning, or the ecosystem position itself. For instance, the valuations of Z.ai and Kimi point to an effective open source strategy, getting traction and growth opportunities in the community. Going forward, however, the industry is likely to shift toward clearer monetization paths from open-source adoption.

Industry observers note that A model’s ecosystem position is not defined only by its own releases, but by how much the community builds on top of it. As mentioned above, Qwen is one exception which is getting attention and adoption.

By this measure, Qwen has become one of the largest foundations in the open model ecosystem. Qwen-based models now account for 151,448 derivatives on the Hub, 2.6× Meta’s total footprint and 4.7× the Llama repositories specifically. Google follows with 82,506 derivatives. The third-largest source is Unsloth, a community account publishing quantized and fine-tuning-ready builds, many of which further extend the Qwen ecosystem.

It has been revealed that qwen derivatives have increased at roughly 180–210 fresh repositories per day throughout the first seven months of 2026, showing that adoption is not driven only by individual launches. Qwen has become part of the default workflow for developers deciding what models to fine-tune and deploy.

Several factors contributed to this position. First, consistency. Qwen has maintained a regular release cadence, continuously updating its model family rather than relying on occasional flagship releases. Second, coverage. It publishes models across a wide range of sizes and use cases, allowing developers to stay within the same ecosystem whether they need a small local model or a larger deployment model. Third, openness. Apache 2.0 licensing reduces friction for modification, redistribution, and commercial use.

Sources indicate that these factors reinforce each other. A broad model family attracts more developers; more developers create more derivatives; and those derivatives make the ecosystem more attractive to future users.

This position was built largely by the community. The 151,448 derivatives represent downstream work created by other developers, not releases produced by Qwen itself. Even among the 28,531 GGUF conversions of Qwen models on the Hub, Qwen published only 54.

Among models that declare a parameter count, those under 1B take 83% of all-time downloads and everything above 100B takes 1%. Restricting to downloads accumulated in 2026 changes nothing: 3% of the volume goes to models above 70B. This is the March finding that has held up most cleanly, for the same reason as before, small models are the only ones that run on the hardware most developers actually have.

Industry observers note that so how does a trillion-parameter model reach anyone at all? Through llama.cpp.

In a recent development, in February the ggml team joined Hugging Face, with the project remaining fully open-source, community-governed and in the same technical direction. What changed is that the most important project in local inference now has durable resources behind it.

The ceiling moved with llama.cpp. The July snapshot carries GGUF builds of DeepSeek-V4-Flash at roughly 284B parameters and Kimi-K3 at roughly 2.8 trillion. Local inference used to mean an 8B model on a laptop. It now means a trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts spread across a few consumer machines, which is the alternative route the frontier did not have a year ago, and the reason a frontier-first release strategy is viable at all.

And that route runs on Qwen: 39.6 million GGUF downloads a month, nearly twice Gemma's 20.8 million and more than five times Llama's 7.5 million. The Llama gap is not a supply problem, Llama-derived GGUF repositories slightly outnumber Qwen's. Same shelf space, a fifth of the traffic.

Model repositories grew 21.5% over these seven months. Several things around them grew several times faster.

Repositories declaring the gguf library rose 464%, lerobot 194% and Apple's mlx148%, against 16% for transformers and peft and 21% for diffusers. The modelling core is growing at roughly the platform average. The layer that decides where a model can physically run local inference formats, Apple silicon, robot control stacks, is growing three to seven times faster than that.

Across the ten largest model families, the labs behind these models publish very few official GGUF conversions. Yet GGUF versions are often the ones used by developers running models locally. Providing an official conversion at release, documenting quantization choices, and signing the artifacts would require limited additional effort. Rather than maintaining this workflow internally, labs could collaborate with existing ecosystem contributors such as Unsloth. Doing so would narrow the gap between the weights tested by model creators and the versions adopted by the broader community.

Industry observers note that we could not have written this section in March, because the instrument did not exist. The agent-usage dataset, published in July, records the agent/ token that coding agents send when they call the Hub through huggingface_hub or the hf CLI — searching for models, pushing datasets, running Jobs, creating Spaces. For the first time we can see how much agent traffic the Hub receives and which harnesses it comes from.

It has been revealed that claude Code led July with 44.4%, but a single month conceals the real finding: it held 67.8% in April and 64% in May, while Codex climbed steadily from 10.4% to 20.8%. This is a market with no incumbent, where one release or one changed default can move half the traffic in a month.

In a recent development, the second finding is the unregistered row. Nearly a quarter of agent-tagged traffic in July came from harnesses not yet named in the dataset, and in May that figure was 59.8%. Between April and July more than a dozen upcoming client identifiers appeared. New entrants are arriving faster than any registry can name them — which is itself the finding.

We spent much of the year building for this reader rather than only for human browsers. Papers began serving machine-readable Markdown in March. April brought agent traces as a first-class dataset type and an agents.md endpoint on every Gradio Space, so an agent can read a Space's API and call it directly. July brought the hf_fs tool on our MCP server, exposing repositories, storage, docs and papers through a single interface in just over a thousand tokens, alongside attachable sandboxes for secure execution. The same consolidation happened at the protocol layer, with MCP moving into the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation.

Then, in July, an agent stopped being a reader and became an intruder. What appears to be the first documented case of an autonomous agent running a sustained intrusion on its own initiative happened to us. While our team tried to use frontier closed models to analyze the captured attack code, their safety guardrails declined the work. The analysis was completed in the end on a quantized open model GLM-5.2 running on our own infrastructure. We published a disclosure and a full technical timeline.

Compared to the spring report, the geographical rebalancing of power continues to accelerate. While U.S. open source models continue to be competitive, the race between several Chinese frontier model labs draws strong attention. Many likes on these frontier models point to what excites the community the most, and growth opportunity for companies leveraging the attention for valuations.

Industry observers note that however, the AI race is not only sprints, but also a marathon; tools like llama.cpp helps deploying the major models locally, but a broad model family and its adoption is still the key, to build a positive feedback loop between developers, publisher and future owners. Models to be embedded in the infrastructure and being part of the ecosystem, may lead to a commercially sound exit at the end of the tunnel.

In the end, with agents being the number 1 user on HF Hub for the first time, the next report may look very different.

In AI, a few months can reshape the ecosystem.

This analysis is based on activity observed on the Hugging Face Hub during the first seven months of 2026.

The metrics used in this report, including downloads, likes, derivatives, and model releases, represent different aspects of ecosystem activity. They should not be interpreted as direct measures of model quality, commercial adoption, or overall market share.

Downloads indicate usage within the Hub ecosystem, but they do not capture API usage, private deployments, or models distributed through other channels.

Likes reflect community attention and interest, while derivative models provide a signal of how much developers build on top of an existing model.

Because open-source AI adoption happens across many channels, Hub activity should be viewed as one perspective on ecosystem development rather than a complete measurement of the AI market.

This article was edited to include latest releases in early August.

Kimi models cannot be served by companies that make more than $20M/year unless explicit authorisation by Moonshot.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the title sounds a bit strange, right? Why re-implement an existing feature, that’s completely useless! I have two reasons for that. The first reason is to be able to adjust the :nth-child() arguments on the fly.

Let’s suppose you have the following:.

And you decide to enhancement the 5 or the 8. The only way is to manually rewrite the selector, which isn’t ideal. We cannot have something like the below where you can change the variables as you want:.

With my implementation, you will be able to do it!

The second reason is to have fun and play with some newly introduced features. You will probably never need to rely on a dynamic :nth-child() selector, but I am sure you will learn one or two useful tricks along the way.

We will rely on the same code structure in all the examples: a container with a bunch of elements inside it.

And the container controls the variables of :nth-child():.

Industry observers note that I am not saying that this structure is mandatory for the implementation. I just considered a simple one to keep things easy to follow.

Let’s start with the simplest case, a selector that selects only one element:.

I don’t think I need to explain what this selector does. The 5 is nothing but the index of the selected element. So, if B is equal to the index of the element, that element is selected.

We can translate this into the following CSS code:.

I am using the newly introduced if() syntax that allows me to define a condition within style(). If that condition is true, the background color is set to red. Otherwise, nothing happens.

Sources indicate that the if() syntax is not that complex. In our case, we only have one condition, so you can see it as follows:.

Recent findings suggest that the tricky part is how to define the condition within style(). I wrote a small post explaining this part, so do yourself a favor and go read it before we continue: “The Hidden Trick of Style Queries and if().” It’s a quick reading with crucial details that helps you better understand how if() works. From there, you will notice that our condition can be written several ways that are all valid:.

Sources indicate that we have our first implementation! You can easily apply it to any property as well:.

According to recent reports, the code looks a bit redundant, which is probably one of the drawbacks of this method, but it’s still cool to implement the selector and be able to adjust the value of --B on the fly. You can have as many as you want combined with and and or.

Now, our selection is more precise.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that google designed TPUs from the ground up to be exceptionally efficient for machine learning workloads, delivering top-tier performance per total cost of ownership (TCO).
  • Performance tuning starts with model definition.
  • The shape rules apply to anyone designing a new model.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that google designed TPUs from the ground up to be exceptionally efficient for machine learning workloads, delivering top-tier performance per total cost of ownership (TCO). Because TPUs trade general-purpose hardware scheduling for wide systolic arrays, dedicated SparseCore engines, and custom interconnect fabrics, adhering to specific architectural best practices is essential to achieve maximum performance. To help developers get the most out of TPUs, we are launching the open-source AI-Hypercomputer/tpu-codesign guide. This post highlights its key principles—spanning shape alignment, architectural choices like LatentMoE, and parallelism strategies—to accelerate LLMs, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, and other hardware-intensive workloads on TPUs.

Performance tuning starts with model definition. Architectural choices made before the first training step set permanent ceilings on MFU (Model FLOP Utilization), cost, and serving latency. This guide gives concrete, hardware-grounded design rules for teams building or adapting models for TPUs, organized into three groups:.

How to use this guide. The shape rules apply to anyone designing a new model. If you are adapting an existing model rather than designing one, the Expressing Parallelism section applies without touching the checkpoint. The general rules hold for any large-matmul architecture (dense LLMs, multimodal, and world models), and the companion AI-Hypercomputer/tpu-codesign repository grows model- and workload-specific sections over time.

Eighth-generation TPUs. These principles carry forward to TPU 8t and TPU 8i and to the newly revealed TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max. The reasoning stays the same and the thresholds move with the hardware. TPU 8t and TPU 8i both add native FP4. For training, TPU 8t also brings more balanced Vector Processing Unit (VPU) scaling. For serving, TPU 8i adds the Boardfly topology, a Collectives Acceleration Engine (CAE), and 3x more on-chip SRAM. We note the effects inline in Principles 5–8, and follow-up posts will cover eighth-generation designs in depth.

Measured evidence. Alongside the published sources, notes marked Measured carry results from our own Ironwood profiling program: open 20–30B MoEs (a Qwen3-30B-derived LatentMoE variant; GPT-OSS-20B) plus dense controls, single slice (except for the 512-chip TPU v7x and 1,024-chip TPU v4 ablations in Principle 4), BF16, training shapes up to 32K sequence, all against tuned-systems baselines. Treat the trends and rankings as transferable, the exact percentages as config-specific.

In a recent development, TPUs are purpose-built custom ML ASICs designed from the ground up to deliver state-of-the-art performance per total cost of ownership (TCO). While their architectural choices—such as wide 256×256 systolic arrays, software-managed VMEM, dedicated SparseCore engines, and direct multi-dimensional ICI fabrics—enable exceptional efficiency, they inherently create specific structural constraints and programming patterns that must be carefully followed to unlock maximal performance. Reaching peak efficiency requires aligning model shapes, routing, and parallelism directly with these underlying hardware characteristics:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At least it’s less disruptive than an internet shutdown.

At 08:30 on Thursday morning every powered-on mobile phone in South Korea blared out an Extreme Emergency Alert tone for 10.5 seconds – but the nation was at peace, with no major natural disasters occurring.

The extreme emergency South Korea hoped to avoid was cheating in the annual College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), an exam that over half a million people sit in the hope of securing admission to their preferred university. This year, around a third of those applicants are repeating the test after their previous effort didn’t get them the result they wanted.

According to recent reports, CSAT involves five separate examinations staged in a single day. Participants can only bring pencils to the test. Smartphones or any sort of tech is strictly forbidden.

Which is why Korean authorities used the national alert system on the day of CSAT, because if the 40dB tone sounded in an exam centre, it could indicate a student had deliberately or inadvertently tried to bring a smartphone – perhaps as an exam aide.

Korean media report the 08:30 alert turned up nine phones.

Authorities will send a second alert tone at an unspecified time later in the day to again smoke out any surreptitious smartphones.

It’s not possible to opt out of the alerts, one reason a concerned netizen has used the Android glitch tracker to suggest sending alerts to detect exam cheats could be an abuse of the emergency alert system that Google might want to do something about.

According to recent reports, south Korea sends a lot of emergency alerts, for matters such as helping to find missing persons or to warn of dangerous weather. It’s not uncommon to receive several in a single day. Authorities also gave advance notice of the CSAT alerts, which will not, therefore, cause panic on the streets of Seoul or Busan.

In a recent development, CSAT day is, however, a serious occasion. Some businesses open late so test-takers can get to their exams without having to battle peak hour traffic.

Those measures are arguably less disruptive than the widespread internet outages that some states in India impose on major exam days.

Industry observers note that an alleged leak of one Indian exam paper saw the nation’s tech regulator ban messaging service Telegram in the country and eventually sparked a youth protest movement that Upcoming Delhi tried to suppress with more deliberate internet outages. ®.

#46784. Latest Update: Same Cluster, 33 Points More Utilization: What Changed Was the Order

📅 17 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2670 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Same Cluster, 33 Points More Utilization: What Changed Was the Order

📅 17 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2670 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the previous post argued that utilization, not intelligence, is where the next real constraint in enterprise AI is forming, and it closed by noting that no playbook has emerged yet for what a mature GPU Management practice looks like.
  • It has been revealed that we built a constraint-aware GPU allocator and benchmarked it against a FIFO scheduler across seven benchmark scenarios.
  • One note on measurement before the numbers start.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the previous post argued that utilization, not intelligence, is where the next real constraint in enterprise AI is forming, and it closed by noting that no playbook has emerged yet for what a mature GPU Management practice looks like. This is ours.

It has been revealed that we built a constraint-aware GPU allocator and benchmarked it against a FIFO scheduler across seven benchmark scenarios. On identical hardware, running identical workloads, GPU utilization rose by as much as 33 percentage points, and priority-weighted output rose in every one of them, by as much as 105%. Nothing about the hardware changed. What changed was the order in which allocation decisions get made.

One note on measurement before the numbers start. Every gain below is expressed as improvement over the FIFO result on the same scenario. Utilization is reported in percentage points; value is reported as a percentage increase in priority-weighted output.

"Keep the GPUs busy" is not a decision a system can execute. The decision is narrower and much harder: which GPU runs which job, in which timestep, at what priority. Formally it is one binary choice per combination of GPU, job and timestep, and the output is a grid — every GPU, across the whole scheduling horizon, with a job name in each cell or nothing at all.

Four workload types compete for that grid: training, real-time inference, batch inference, and quantization. They split into two allocation shapes, and the split is where the difficulty lives. Training, batch inference and quantization are batch-like: once started, each needs a contiguous block of GPUs held without interruption until the job finishes. Real-time inference is the opposite: elastic, driven by a demand curve that changes every timestep, growing and shrinking as traffic does.

Industry observers note that two incompatible shapes competing for the same hardware in the same timestep is the core problem. A second heterogeneity sits inside a single type: for the same base model, training jobs range from a few hours to several days, and from one GPU to dozens.

The comparison point throughout is a FIFO-based scheduler: real-time inference served from a fixed reservation, and every other job placed in arrival order, without regard for priority.

Sources indicate that under the right conditions, that is a reasonable policy. When the cluster has slack, allocation order costs nothing in utilization, everything fits regardless of sequence, so FIFO and anything more sophisticated fill the same fraction of the pool. Contention is where that ordering cost stops being invisible and starts costing capacity too. It then becomes expensive in two separate ways, and they are worth taking one at a time.

Recent findings suggest that the reservation. Real-time inference cannot wait for capacity; the GPUs have to be there the moment traffic needs them. A scheduler that places jobs in arrival order has no mechanism for releasing GPUs during a trough and reclaiming them before the next peak, so the only way to guarantee availability is to take each real-time application's maximum demand for the day and reserve that many GPUs for the whole day. The cost lands in every hour that is not the peak. An application needing six GPUs at midday and two at 4am holds all six for twenty-four hours, and the four idle GPUs are unavailable to any batch job for the entire day. They are not being used, and they are not free either. It is why the baseline sits near half the cluster in the two scenarios where reservation dominates: 51.6% in the mixed control and 53.6% in the training-heavy case. Roughly half a pool, with much of the idle half reserved rather than free. This cost is paid whether the cluster is contended or not — contention only makes it visible.

Sources indicate that the ordering. Under real contention, which jobs fit at all depends on the order you place them, not just on how much capacity exists. Order is not a tiebreaker applied after the capacity question is settled. Order is a capacity decision. FIFO places each job as it arrives, without weighing what that job is worth and without checking what else still has to fit inside the horizon, so high-priority work waits behind whatever asked first and capacity gets committed in placements that later jobs cannot use.

It has been revealed that the two compound. The block held for the day's maximum real-time demand is off the table for every batch job in the queue, in every hour, and whatever remains is handed out in the order the requests happened to arrive.

Sources indicate that it is the GPU equivalent of an airline assigning aircraft to whichever charter called first, then finding nothing left to fly the route that actually pays. And GPUs reserved all day for a peak lasting a couple of hours are the grounded aircraft from the previous piece in the most literal sense: on standby, earning nothing, unavailable to anyone else.

[Figure: side-by-side allocation grids — allocator above, FIFO below, same scenario].

Across five benchmark scenarios built for genuine contention, the allocator improved both axes at once. Utilization moved from a 52–85% band to a 72–88% band. Priority-weighted value rose between 24.6% and 105.1%, averaging 52%. Every scenario, both metrics, no tradeoff to explain away.

The strongest single case was a training-heavy workload on 8 GPUs: utilization went from 53.6% to 87.0%, and value more than doubled, up 105%. Thirty-three points of a fixed, already-depreciating asset, recovered by reclaiming reserved standby capacity and placing the rest in priority order. (This figure reflect a single baseline ordering.).

Sources indicate that the allocator removes both behaviors. Real-time demand is treated as a curve rather than a ceiling, allocated against demand at each timestep, with batch-like work occupying the troughs, bounded by the cap on how many GPUs a real-time job may swap between consecutive timesteps. And batch-like jobs are placed by priority across the whole horizon instead of in the order they arrived. The rest of this piece is how.

Industry observers note that utilization measures occupancy: what fraction of available GPU-time is allocated to something. It carries no information about what that something is worth. One scenario pulls the two apart completely, and the gap runs in a direction that is easy to miss.

Recent findings suggest that in the scale test, 30 jobs across 64 GPUs, FIFO and the allocator produced identical utilization, 44.9% each, and identical throughput, 27 of 30 jobs completed. The allocator delivered 15.9% more priority-weighted value. Every dashboard reads the same. The cluster produced materially different output.

An objective that does not price priority can fill the cluster to exactly the same level, finish exactly as many jobs, and still deliver less. The previous piece argued that occupancy is a poor read on whether a cluster is earning; this is the measured version of that claim.

Recent findings suggest that the alternative is not a longer list of heuristic rules. Some constraints only mean anything globally, and no local rule can express them: contiguous blocks, a budget for how much GPU churn is acceptable across the entire horizon, a guarantee that running work is never preempted. To honor those, the problem has to be written down as one thing.

Five constraints define a legal allocation:.

The objective function has two terms. Allocating a GPU to a batch-like job earns a reward equal to its priority multiplied by a time-decay weight. Failing to meet real-time demand incurs a penalty proportional to the size of the shortfall.

The relative size of those weights is the entire service-level policy, expressed as one number. The real-time penalty weight is 5 to 10 times greater than the allocation weight. One unit of unmet real-time demand therefore costs what 5 to 10 GPU-timesteps of equal-priority batch work costs. The asymmetry is deliberate, and it means latency obligations are enforced inside the same optimization that places batch work, rather than by a separate autoscaler competing with the scheduler for the same GPUs.

It is also what makes the elastic treatment of real-time demand safe. The allocator can hand a GPU to batch work during a trough because underserving real-time demand later is priced so far above whatever that batch work earns — the penalty, not a static reservation, is what protects availability.

According to recent reports, the time weight decays across the horizon for a reason that only makes sense in an online system: by the next scheduling run, upcoming jobs will have arrived. Capacity used now is worth more than capacity promised later.

The formal model defines what a legal, well-scored allocation looks like. Answering an incoming request is a separate job, and it belongs to a separate component. This is NP-hard combinatorial allocation, and the scheduler is re-invoked every time a job arrives, so the decision has to come back in the gap between two API requests. That latency budget is the fixed constraint the architecture is designed around, which is why a heuristic sits on the hot path and the formal model sits behind it as the specification the heuristic is built to satisfy.

Industry observers note that that heuristic is not a generic greedy allocator. Its rules are the formal model's structural constraints, which means every grid it produces is a legal allocation by construction. Not usually valid. Valid by design.

According to recent reports, that design, applied across the whole horizon rather than one arrival at a time, is what produces the utilization gain. The allocator sees every queued job before it places any of them, it can hold the free pool in shapes the remaining work can actually occupy, a batch job needing a contiguous block of a given size still has room when its turn comes. Priority decides who gets first claim on that room. FIFO has neither view: it commits capacity to whichever job asked first, and a job that arrives later and needs a specific shape may find nothing left that fits, so it goes unscheduled and the GPU-hours it would have consumed go unclaimed.

It runs in 1 to 2 milliseconds on the five contended scenarios, and 15 milliseconds at 64 GPUs and 30 jobs — fast enough to run on every incoming request.

The system exposes two modes. Fast mode runs the allocator alone and returns its grid; this is the hot path. Full mode uses that grid as a starting point for the formal model, which attempts to improve on it — suited to periodic review rather than per-request decisions.

Sources indicate that utilization improved in every scenario but one, where it tied exactly. Value improved in all seven.

The scale test matters because it holds at size: 64 GPUs, 30 jobs, 15 milliseconds, 15.9% more value.

Industry observers note that the uniform-priority test matters because it addresses the obvious skeptical reading. Override every job to identical priority, so that no priority signal distinguishes any of them, and the allocator still moves utilization from 76.8% to 87.5% and value up 23.1%. The gain is not purely an artifact of ordering by priority. Planning placements across the horizon contributes on its own.

Everything above assumes the scheduler knows how many GPU-hours each job needs and how much real-time traffic is coming. Both are predictions, not inputs, and a scheduler is only as good as they are.

Recent findings suggest that A single generic estimator does not work, because the four workload types have qualitatively different cost drivers. This is where the specialization argument from the previous piece reconnects: the same logic that makes a task-specific model outperform a generalist applies to the estimators feeding the scheduler.

Sources indicate that training is not one workload. It varies along two independent, freely combinable axes. Strategy determines how much of the model is updated (full fine-tuning against parameter-efficient methods like LoRA). Technique determines the optimization objective and the training loop (SFT, DPO, RLHF, RLVR, CPT). The differences are not marginal: LoRA cuts trainable parameters by up to 10,000× and GPU memory roughly 3× against full fine-tuning, on the same base model. DPO removes both the reward model and the sampling loop of RLHF. Estimating from model size alone averages across runs that differ by orders of magnitude, in exactly the two quantities the scheduler decides on, duration and GPU count. Our training forecaster conditions on 22 features, including a categorical variable distinguishing 10 concrete training variants.

Quantization is a schedulable job, not a background chore. Quantizing a single large model can consume hours of GPU time on hardware that other work is waiting for. It gets its own forecast, built from calibration tiers by parameter count, with distinct handling per algorithm (bitsandbytes, AWQ, GPTQ) and a safety margin before rounding up to whole GPU-hours. Prior work in this area places quantization outside scheduling scope entirely.

Real-time inference is not estimated per job at all. It is forecast as a continuously recalibrated weekly demand profile, rebuilt from hourly traffic history and mapped to GPU counts under the same swap cost the formal model enforces. Forecast and optimizer therefore agree on what churn costs, rather than disagreeing and fighting each other. This forecast is what replaces peak reservation. A per-timestep demand curve is the only thing that lets the scheduler release GPUs during a trough with any confidence that they can be reclaimed before the next peak.

This closes back to the ordering argument. Better demand estimates are what make priority-aware placement possible in the first place, you cannot sequence jobs well without knowing what they will consume.

According to recent reports, the obvious objection to all of this is that forecasts are wrong. What happens then?

The failure mode to avoid has a name worth borrowing: the end-of-world effect. An optimizer that cannot see past the end of its horizon makes present decisions that wreck the timesteps immediately outside it, because as far as the model is concerned, nothing exists after the horizon ends.

The architecture answers both problems at once. The scheduler optimizes a 24-hour horizon, but commits only the current timestep, and re-runs every 30 to 60 minutes. Run at 9am, and the 9am allocation is real; the plan for 10am through 5pm exists only so that the 9am decision is made by a model that knows a future exists. The real 10am allocation comes from the 10am run, against fresh data.

Recent findings suggest that the consequence is that forecast error is absorbed by re-optimization instead of compounding. Each run inherits what is actually running and pins it in place, so successive plans update rather than thrash.

Industry observers note that there is a secondary payoff. The horizon plan is itself a forecasting product: it surfaces real-time coverage risk and predictable idle windows before they arrive, which is useful whether or not those specific allocations are ever committed.

This is also why the time-decay weight exists. By the next run, the workload mix will have changed.

Airlines did not solve utilization by computing an optimal schedule. They solved it by encoding operational discipline into the order things happen (turnaround sequence, maintenance windows, crew rostering) and letting that discipline compound.

The same thing happened here. Thirty-three points of utilization in the hardest-packed scenario, and 52% more priority-weighted output on average, on the same hardware, with the same workloads, in a couple of milliseconds, came from encoding what the cluster physically permits into the order decisions get made. Structure beat sophistication.

According to recent reports, the previous piece argued that specialization and orchestration are two halves of one problem: specialization shrinks what each workload needs, and orchestration decides where the difference goes. Neither lever pays off alone. This is what the second half looks like when it is built.

The GPUs were already installed, already committed, already depreciating. The gain was in how we chose to spend them.
