💡 Key Takeaways
  • CSS can now make choices about type that used to sit outside a reset.
  • I’ve put together tidy-typography.css, which gathers the useful parts into a default stylesheet: rendering and fallback rules, fluid sizing, vertical rhythm, wrapping, hyphenation, and OpenType detail.
  • Use it whole, or take the declaration that solves the particular irritation in front of you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CSS can now make choices about type that used to sit outside a reset. text-wrap: pretty can prevent a stranded word, container query units can scale a heading to the column it occupies, and text-box can trim the half-leading built into a line box. Some of these features are experimental and browser support is uneven, so they need guardrails rather than blind inclusion.

I’ve put together tidy-typography.css, which gathers the useful parts into a default stylesheet: rendering and fallback rules, fluid sizing, vertical rhythm, wrapping, hyphenation, and OpenType detail.

Use it whole, or take the declaration that solves the particular irritation in front of you. I’ll walk you through all the details in this article and give you the full code at the end.

It has been revealed that font-synthesis: none stops a browser from inventing bold or italic when the family lacks that face. The smoothing and text-rendering declarations are rendering hints, mainly for WebKit; results still vary by platform.

text-size-adjust disables mobile font inflation that can make a deliberately sized layout jump on rotation. font-size-adjust: from-font uses font metrics to reduce the apparent size change while a fallback swaps for a webfont.

(As with other snippets in this article, this ⁠:root block is a partial excerpt the final stylesheet combines it with additional custom properties defined later on.).

Recent findings suggest that viewport-based fluid type does not know how wide its element is. A heading in a narrow sidebar can therefore scale as though it fills the viewport.

Recent findings suggest that container-type: inline-size makes the wrapper a container query, so its children can use cqi: a unit based on the container rather than the viewport. Replacing vw in clamp() lets the same heading scale appropriately in an article column or a 300px sidebar without component-specific media queries.

It has been revealed that line-height includes space above the cap-height and below the baseline: half-leading. It becomes obvious when text must align tightly with another element. text-box-trim removes it, while text-box-edge measures from capital-letter caps to the alphabetic baseline. This is a metrics-aware alternative to font-specific negative-margin nudges.

Selectors Level 5 proposes :heading, matching h1 to h6 and [role="heading"]. It has not landed in browsers, so keep it behind an @supports selector() check.

Sources indicate that default heading wrapping can leave one short final line. text-wrap: balance distributes text across its lines and works best for blocks of up to about six lines. For paragraphs, text-wrap: pretty avoids a stranded final word without balancing the whole block. Both replace JavaScript orphan fixers. Editable text needs text-wrap: stable, which prevents each newly introduced word from reshuffling the paragraph.

Industry observers note that hyphens: auto relies on the browser’s language dictionaries, so the document needs a correct lang attribute (for example ). Without one the browser has no dictionary to use and won’t be able to hyphenate text. Even with the correct lang, the defaults can leave tiny word fragments or several hyphenated lines in a row.

hyphenate-limit-chars controls the smallest breakable word and fragments; hyphenate-limit-lines prevents a ladder effect. hyphenate-limit-zone makes breaks less frequent, while hyphenate-limit-last protects the final word. Safari needs the prefixed equivalents, so declare both sets together.

Set code, variables, and headings to hyphens: manual: a broken code word can change meaning, and a hyphenated heading usually reads as an error.

Recent findings suggest that punctuation marks don’t carry the same visual weight as letters, so a quotation mark sitting at the start of a line can look slightly indented against the text below it. hanging-punctuation lets specified punctuation sit fractionally outside the text block’s edge.

In a recent development, the first value handles opening punctuation, and last handles closing punctuation at the end of a block, while allow-end lets punctuation hang past the right edge rather than force-wrapping. The result is a text block whose edges read as genuinely flush.

Underlines have a related problem. Browsers apply flat, one-size-fits-all thickness and position regardless of the font’s actual weight.

text-decoration-thickness: from-font reads the thickness the font’s designer intended. text-underline-offset gives descenders room to breathe, and text-decoration-skip-ink: auto interrupts the underline wherever a descender crosses it rather than drawing straight through the letter.

According to recent reports, variable fonts often include an optical size axis, or opsz. It lets a typeface use thinner strokes at large display sizes and thicker, more legible strokes when set small.

Sources indicate that font-optical-sizing: auto lets the font make that adjustment based on its actual rendered size. The @supports block covers the older font-variation-settings syntax some browsers still need, while font-variant-ligatures and font-kerning enable the font’s own ligatures and kerning pairs.

Light text on a dark background genuinely reads heavier than the same weight on a light background. Where a font ships a GRAD, or grade, axis, the dark mode block dials that perceived weight down without changing glyph shape or width the way an actual weight change would. Fonts without a GRAD axis safely ignore the setting.

According to recent reports, mixing a monospace font into running prose often exposes a mismatched x-height at the same declared font-size. The size-adjust keyword, set once at the @font-face level, scales that font’s rendered output specifically, leaving the actual font-size value untouched.

According to recent reports, numbers in a table need identical widths so they stack into a clean column on the screen. Conversely, numbers in flowing text don’t need the same treatment and should sit naturally alongside the surrounding words.

According to recent reports, the tabular-nums and lining-nums keywords give table digits a fixed width and full cap height. oldstyle-nums and proportional-nums let digits sit alongside lowercase letters without sticking up and disrupting the sentence’s texture.

font-variant-emoji makes the choice between full-colour and monochrome emoji explicit. Without it, the browser or platform gets to choose a fallback, and the result can vary more than you expect. Apply .emoji-color or .emoji-mono to containers where you want to enforce that choice, rather than setting it globally on the body.

Quote style and character order differ by language and region. English nests single quotes inside double quotes, British English reverses that convention, and French uses guillemets with a thin space.

The quotes property declares the order for each language through :lang(). The native q element then inserts the right pair through open-quote and close-quote. The same markup can render correctly in each locale without hardcoding characters into the content.

Wrapping the rules in :where() keeps them at zero specificity, so a project can override the quote style with one plain class.

Default sub and sup styling is synthesized. The browser just shrinks the text and shifts the baseline, rather than using glyphs actually designed for that position.

Industry observers note that font-variant-position switches to the font’s own purpose-built sub and superscript glyphs where they exist, resetting vertical-align, font-size, and line-height so they don’t fight against the real glyph’s intended size and position. Most typefaces only include proper numerals rather than letters, so check the specific font before applying this broadly.

:where() always resolves to zero specificity, which is useful for a reset. Every rule here is an opinionated default, and wrapping it in :where() lets a project override a property with a plain class.

Sources indicate that :is() solves a different problem: repetition. The heading selector list appears several times in a typographic stylesheet, and grouping it avoids the risk of forgetting a level.

Unlike :where(), :is() carries the specificity of its most specific argument.

Sources indicate that here’s the complete reset, combining the stable layers. Unsupported declarations are ignored by the browser, so the stylesheet can be adopted gradually.

Recent findings suggest that much of this CSS removes work that used to leak into other parts of a build. text-wrap can take over orphan handling from JavaScript, container query units keep a component’s type scale tied to its own width, and text-box-trim avoids the negative margins once used to compensate for leading. quotes, font-variant-position, and font-optical-sizing hand several smaller details back to the language and the font instead of a collection of one-off fixes.

Sources indicate that browser support will continue to change, especially for text-wrap and text-box-trim. Unsupported declarations are ignored, but that only helps when the unenhanced typography is acceptable in its own right.

It has been revealed that some of these rules are still too new for a baseline reset. A news article, a marketing page, and an editable product interface do not ask the same things of their text; the set that belongs in yours depends on the font, the content, and the browsers you still need to support.

#46782. GTA VI didn't break the internet, thanks to 'stupid DNS tricks'

GTA VI didn't break the internet, thanks to 'stupid DNS tricks'

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (477 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Multiple CDNs and routing customers to nearby download sites kept traffic flowing for everyone.
  • Grand Theft Auto VI may put a dent in global productivity today but the game didn’t break the internet.
  • For those unfamiliar, GTA VI is the first new instalment of the mega-hit game in 13 years and it is nearly impossible to understate the excitement surrounding its release.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Multiple CDNs and routing customers to nearby download sites kept traffic flowing for everyone.

Grand Theft Auto VI may put a dent in global productivity today but the game didn’t break the internet.

For those unfamiliar, GTA VI is the first new instalment of the mega-hit game in 13 years and it is nearly impossible to understate the excitement surrounding its release. Anecdotal evidence suggests fans of the game may today report they suddenly feel unfit to perform paid work.

Developer Rockstar Games allowed Xbox and PlayStation owners to pay for and download the 200GB-plus game on November 10, before play commenced on the 19th.

Millions took advantage of the chance to download the game, creating just the sort of internet traffic event that regional internet registry the Réseaux IP Européens Network Coordination Centre (RIPE NCC) can observe with its RIPE Atlas internet measurement network.

RIPE data scientist Emile Aben, with help from staffers Alun Davies and James Cowie, went looking for GTA-related traffic and found some interesting patterns.

It has been revealed that aben observed that traffic to PlayStations mostly came from content delivery networks operated by AWS and Fastly. Microsoft relied on Fastly for over half of traffic flowing to Xboxes and used Akamai too, but eschewed AWS's CloudFront.

It has been revealed that the data scientist observed heavy use of “GeoDNS,” a technique that returns different IP addresses for a single domain request, depending on a user’s location. DNS’s designers didn’t intend that. Indeed, the RIPE trio point out that Paul Vixie, the computer scientist who earned his place in the Internet Hall of Fame for massive contributions to the DNS system, regarded things like GeoDNS as “stupid DNS tricks.”.

Whatever you think of GeoDNS, the RIPE researchers found that folks who were likely downloading GTA VI from Los Angeles, Tokyo, and Istanbul were each directed to different sites.

Their probe of a network in Shanghai, China, found “a very distinct long lookup-chain with a hostname that is associated with the Alibaba Cloud in the end that maps to six different IP addresses.”.

“This hints at specialised treatment for some countries/regions,” Aben wrote.

He also noted that Internet Exchange Points, the interconnect facilities that network operators use to exchange traffic and shorten paths, had to cope with record traffic during the download period – and seem to have handled the load.

Aben thinks the GTA VI download program offers a useful lesson.

Sources indicate that “DNS helps steer each player towards a download server, while multiple CDNs share the work of delivering the files,” he wrote. “That distribution matters beyond gaming. On the open Internet, game downloads share routers and link capacity with all kinds of other traffic, including critical services.”.

“Keeping downloads local helps leave capacity on long-distance links free for other uses, making that enormous demand manageable.” ®.

Multi-Vector (Late Interaction) Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers

📅 18 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 28 min read (5589 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~28 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more.
  • According to recent reports, where a regular embedding model compresses a whole text into one vector, a multi-vector model keeps one vector per token and scores query against document with the MaxSim operator.
  • In this blogpost, we'll show you how to use these models: loading the various checkpoint formats, encoding and scoring, plugging them into a search stack, running them on page images, and keeping the index affordable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more. With the v6.0 revision, it gains a fourth model type: MultiVectorEncoder, for ColBERT-style late interaction retrieval. Any PyLate checkpoint and any Stanford-NLP ColBERT checkpoint loads straight into it, and colpali-engine models for visual document retrieval can be used too, through the same familiar API you already use for dense, sparse, and reranker models.

According to recent reports, where a regular embedding model compresses a whole text into one vector, a multi-vector model keeps one vector per token and scores query against document with the MaxSim operator. That preserves token-level matching information that a single vector has to average away, which usually means stronger retrieval at the cost of a bigger index. It's also the state of the art for visual document retrieval, where a text query is matched against page images directly, with no OCR step in between.

In this blogpost, we'll show you how to use these models: loading the various checkpoint formats, encoding and scoring, plugging them into a search stack, running them on page images, and keeping the index affordable. Everything below runs on a plain pip install -U sentence-transformers.

This blog is about using multi-vector models. If you want to learn how to train them, see the companion Training and Finetuning Multi-Vector Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers blogpost.

A dense embedding model reads a text and returns a single fixed-size vector. Everything the model noticed has to fit in those 384, 768, or 1024 numbers, and similarity is one dot product between two such summaries. This works remarkably well, but the compression is lossy in a specific way: a rare entity, an exact identifier, or one crucial clause in a long passage all have to compete for room in the same vector. A query with several requirements at once runs into the same wall. For "green sofa with wooden legs and rounded cushions", a single vector has to blend all four into one point, so a green sofa with the wrong legs ends up sitting close to the one you actually asked for.

Industry observers note that A multi-vector model (also called a late-interaction or ColBERT-style model, after the ColBERT paper) skips that compression. It runs the same transformer, but instead of pooling the token embeddings into one vector, it projects each token embedding down to a small dimension (classically 128) and keeps all of them. A 9-token document becomes a 9x128 matrix, not a 1x128 vector.

Sources indicate that the interaction between query and document is then deferred until scoring time, which is where the name "late interaction" comes from. A cross-encoder interacts early, with both texts going through the model together, which is accurate but leaves nothing to precompute, since every document has to be re-encoded for each new query. A bi-encoder, which is what the dense embedding model above is, barely interacts at all (one dot product between two finished summaries), and that is exactly what lets you encode a collection once and query it fast. Late interaction sits in between. Documents are still encoded independently and can be indexed offline, but scoring compares every query token against every document token, which leaves far more room for the two to interact.

Scoring uses MaxSim: for each query token, take its highest similarity against any document token, then sum those maxima across the query.

MaxSim(Q,D)=∑Qi∈Qmax⁡Dj∈DQi⋅Dj\text{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{Q_i \in Q} \max_{D_j \in D} Q_i \cdot D_jMaxSim(Q,D)=Qi​∈Q∑​Dj​∈Dmax​Qi​⋅Dj​.

Because the token embeddings are L2-normalized, each of those dot products is a cosine similarity in [-1, 1], so the whole sum lands within [-num_query_tokens, num_query_tokens].

You can read the operator as a soft alignment, where every query token points at the one document token that best explains it, and the score is how well the document supports the query overall.

The alignment doesn't have to be lexical, since the token embeddings are contextualized. Encode "Where do penguins live?" against "Penguins inhabit Antarctica." with lightonai/mLateOn and the query token live finds its best match on inhabit at 0.94, a word it shares no characters with! That is the thing lexical retrieval cannot do, BM25 and its relatives need the term itself, so synonyms and paraphrases slip past them. Dense embedding models bridge that gap as well, of course. What late interaction adds is that it does so without giving up the other direction. When an exact match is what matters (a product code, a surname, a function name), MaxSim still has that token sitting there on its own, where a single-vector model had to average it in with everything else. It isn't one-to-one either, since several query tokens routinely settle on the same document token.

You gain retrieval quality, particularly on queries where one specific piece of a document is what makes it relevant, on multi-requirement queries like the sofa above where each requirement gets to find its own evidence, and on out-of-domain data where a dense model's compression was tuned for a different distribution. That compression is learned from the training queries, so the model learns to keep what they needed and drop everything else, which may include exactly what your production queries ask about. The effect grows with document length, since more text has to fit in the same fixed vector.

It has been revealed that the cost is index size. One vector per token instead of one vector per document is a lot more vectors, only partly offset by the smaller dimension. Encoding 4,874 Natural Questions passages with lightonai/LateOn produced 608,414 token vectors, an average of 124.8 per passage:.

Recent findings suggest that that's about 42x the storage of the MiniLM index, or 62 KiB per passage. However, indexes are often compressed, e.g. the same 608,414 vectors take 92 MB as a fast-plaid index, since PLAID stores a centroid id plus a quantized residual per vector rather than the vector itself. For scale, a 4096-dimensional dense model like Qwen3-Embedding-8B would need about 80 MB for these same 4,874 passages, so a compressed multi-vector index sits in the same territory as the dense indexes people already run. Token Pooling cuts the vector count before any of that, and Retrieve and Rerank avoids building an index at all.

PyLate comes up throughout this post, so here is the short version. Sentence Transformers handled dense and sparse models but not late interaction, so LightOn built PyLate on top of it to close that gap, adding the training, inference, and retrieval pieces these models need. Much of what you'll load below was trained with it, and LightOn built an ecosystem around it too, including fast-plaid, the late-interaction index that turns up in Indexing. With v6.0 those capabilities live in Sentence Transformers itself.

With the tradeoff in mind, let's get a model running.

Multi-vector models work with a plain install:.

For ColPali-style visual document retrieval, you also need the image dependencies (see Installation for all extras, and Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models for multimodal support in general):.

Sentence Transformers v6.0 requires transformers v5.x, torch 2.2+, and huggingface-hub v1.x. If you pin any of those lower, initiative the upgrade first. See the Migration Guide for the full list of breaking changes.

Loading a multi-vector model looks exactly like loading any other Sentence Transformers model:.

To find models that work, look for the multi-vector and sentence-transformers tags on the Hub. Any model with those tags loads with the line above, whether it started life as a PyLate checkpoint, a Stanford-NLP ColBERT checkpoint, or a ColPali-family model for visual document retrieval. We're working through the ecosystem to get that tag onto every model that works, so the list keeps growing.

Underneath, MultiVectorEncoder reads each of the formats these checkpoints have been published in over the years, so PyLate and Stanford-NLP checkpoints load directly even where the tag hasn't been added yet:.

Sources indicate that visual document retrieval models are the exception. ColPali-family checkpoints ship in colpali-engine's own format, which carries no information Sentence Transformers can use, so each one needs a small configuration added to its repository before it loads. Most of that work is done and waiting to be merged. See Supported Models for the current state and how to load them today.

In a recent development, multi-vector models carry a handful of recipe knobs that differ per checkpoint: marker prefixes for queries and documents, length caps, whether queries are padded out with [MASK] tokens, and which tokens are skipped when scoring documents. All of them live in the module configs, so print(model) shows you exactly what you loaded. Here's the original ColBERTv2 checkpoint, which pads every query to exactly 32 tokens and truncates documents at 180:.

Industry observers note that that's the classic ColBERT pipeline: a Transformer producing contextualized token embeddings, a token-level Dense projecting each of them to 128 dimensions, a MultiVectorMask deciding which tokens count during scoring, and a token-level Normalize. Other checkpoints fill in different values. lightonai/GTE-ModernColBERT-v1 uses the same four modules with [Q] and [D] prompts, no query expansion, and caps of 48 and 300.

You rarely need to touch any of this, since every released checkpoint configures its own. It matters when you build a model from a bare backbone, which is covered in Creating Custom Models.

Industry observers note that one value is worth checking against your own data, though. document_length truncates, so anything past it never reaches the index. For example, a 662-token passage through LateOn's cap of 300 comes back as 273 vectors, with the rest of the passage simply gone. Most of these checkpoints were trained on short passages, so if your chunks are longer than the cap, you can lift it for a single call with encode_document(..., processing_kwargs={"text": {"max_length": 512}}), keeping in mind that you would be running the model past the length it was trained on and that the index grows roughly in proportion. Multi-vector models tend to tolerate that well. On MLDR, a long-document retrieval benchmark, the multilingual siblings of the pair above show the gap clearly: mLateOn scores 77.92 against mDenseOn's 51.59.

Multi-vector models are asymmetric, so queries and documents go through different prefixes, different length caps, and different scoring masks. Unlike many dense models, where the two are interchangeable, encode_query() and encode_document() are required to get correct embeddings:.

According to recent reports, what you get back is a list of 2D tensors, one per input, each of shape (num_tokens, embedding_dim). Unlike dense embeddings, you can't stack these into one rectangular tensor, because every input has its own token count. The second document is longer than the first, so it comes back as a taller matrix.

It has been revealed that each call applies the model's own recipe for you. encode_query prepends the query marker, expands the query to a fixed length if the checkpoint asks for it, and caps it at the query length. encode_document prepends the document marker, caps at the document length, and drops any skiplisted tokens (punctuation, for most checkpoints) from the scoring mask.

The usual encode() arguments all still apply, so batch_size, show_progress_bar, convert_to_numpy, device, and multi-process pools work the way you'd expect:.

model.similarity() computes the full all-pairs MaxSim matrix:.

Mars wins, as it should, though the runners-up are close behind. Saturn also contains the literal phrase "the Red Planet", and Jupiter is a planet with a red spot, so a token-level operator has plenty to latch onto in all three. The ordering is what matters.

Scores often sit this close together, as GLInt shows by measuring the spread across a full candidate pool. MaxSim takes a maximum per query token, so a document will usually give every query token some decent best match, and scores start from a floor. Contextualized token embeddings are also anisotropic, clustering in a narrow cone rather than spreading out, so even arbitrary token pairs tend to score high.

There is also model.similarity_pairwise(), for when you already have matched pairs and just want the pair scores instead of the full similarity matrix:.

MaxSim sums over query tokens, so its magnitude scales with how many query tokens there are, which means you can't compare scores across models with different query recipes. LateOn encodes the Red Planet query above as 12 tokens. Run that same query and those same documents through ColBERTv2, which pads and truncates every query to exactly 32 tokens, and the scores land in a completely different range:.

Within one model the ordering is all you need, but if you want scores on a bounded scale, switch the model's similarity function to MeanMaxSim, which divides by the query token count. Back on LateOn:.

Now every score is an average cosine similarity in [-1, 1], although you'll only see [0, 1] in practice.

If your corpus is small, exhaustive MaxSim over all of it is the simplest thing that works. Encode the corpus once, then score each query against everything:.

Those 4,874 passages encoded in 20 seconds on an RTX 3090, and each search takes about 120ms end to end, most of that the MaxSim scoring against all 608,414 token vectors. This is exact, but it scales linearly in total corpus tokens and keeps every token vector in memory, so reach for it when you have a few thousand documents rather than a few million. The runnable version of this script is semantic_search.py.

It has been revealed that past that size you want a real late-interaction index, which Sentence Transformers doesn't ship. It doesn't need to, because these indexes store whatever encode_document produced, so you encode here and hand the token embeddings to something built for them. Indexing has working snippets for four of the options, and the section directly below covers how to skip the index entirely.

In a recent development, you can also get late-interaction quality without maintaining a late-interaction index, by using a multi-vector model as your reranker. A fast bi-encoder narrows a large corpus to a handful of candidates, then the multi-vector model rescores only those:.

Only the 50 candidates are ever encoded as multi-vectors, so your index stays a normal dense index and the token vectors are transient. This is the same role a cross-encoder plays in a retrieve-and-rerank stack, but a multi-vector model is considerably cheaper per candidate. You encode the documents in one batch and score them with a matrix multiplication, instead of one forward pass per query-document pair. The runnable script is retrieve_rerank.py, which prints the timings of both stages.

It has been revealed that several vector databases index and score multi-vectors natively: Qdrant since v1.10, Weaviate since v1.29, Vespa for years now, LanceDB since v0.15.0, and VectorChord, which adds a MaxSim operator to Postgres that plain pgvector doesn't have. Milvus joined them in v2.6.4, under array-of-structs rather than the unrelated feature it calls multi-vector search. If you would rather not run a server at all, LightOn's fast-plaid is a pip install away and implements PLAID directly, and PyLate wraps it in a fuller retrieval stack.

It has been revealed that A few others get you partway. OpenSearch and Elasticsearch can rescore candidates with MaxSim but not retrieve on it, and the Elasticsearch field is additionally in technical preview and Enterprise-tier. turbopuffer has late-interaction indexing in private beta.

According to recent reports, the snippets below index text, but nothing in them is text-specific. encode_document hands back the same list of token-vector matrices whether the document was a passage, a page image, an audio clip, or a video, so the ColPali-style models from Visual Document Retrieval go into any of these unchanged. There are simply more vectors per document, which is what makes Token Pooling worth reaching for sooner there.

In a recent development, fast-plaid, Qdrant, Weaviate, and Vespa all take exactly what encode_document returns, so the code is the same up to the client library. Here's a working snippet for each, run against the 4,874 passages and 608,414 token vectors from the Semantic Search example. Each one carries the ingestion and query times it produced on one machine (RTX 3090, i7-13700K), with no tuning beyond what the code shows, to give a sense of the shape of the work. All four answer the query faster than the 98ms model.similarity took in that section, and three of them do it on the CPU, since fast-plaid is the only one here using the GPU.

According to recent reports, all four returned the same three passages in the same order as the exhaustive PyTorch MaxSim earlier in this post, and the three databases reproduce its scores to four decimals! That is because their snippets score every document, which is affordable at this size and removes approximation as a variable. fast-plaid is approximate by design, so its scores differ slightly. The notes under each one say what changes when you switch to an approximate index, which is where rankings start to drift.

fast-plaid is LightOn's Rust implementation of PLAID, the index ColBERT was originally built around. There's no server to start, and it reads the tensors encode_document hands back without any conversion.

It has been revealed that the index argument is a directory, not just a label, so the index is written to disk as it is built. Pointing a newly introduced FastPlaid at the same path reopens it for searching or for adding more documents, instead of rebuilding from the embeddings each time. On this corpus it occupies 92 MB, against 311.5 MB for the raw float32 vectors.

This is the only one of the four that is approximate, and it is the one place in this section where the scores do not match the exhaustive MaxSim. PLAID prunes with centroids and stores quantized residuals, so the three scores drift by a few hundredths in both directions against the 11.9192 / 11.7591 / 11.6710 computed earlier. The ranking is unaffected here, and that is the trade PLAID is making. It was designed for corpora far larger than this one, where scanning everything is not an option.

Industry observers note that qdrant needs a server: docker run -p 6333:6333 qdrant/qdrant. The client also has a local mode (QdrantClient(":memory:")) that needs no server, but it's a pure-Python reimplementation, so use it for trying things out rather than for timing them.

MAX_SIM is the only comparator Qdrant offers, and hnsw_config=HnswConfigDiff(m=0) is their recommendation for late-interaction fields, since the vectors are used for rescoring rather than graph traversal. Note that Qdrant themselves suggest reserving late interaction for reranking a few hundred candidates rather than scanning a whole collection, which is the Retrieve and Rerank pattern. At 4,874 documents the full scan costs 18ms and is exact, but that doesn't extrapolate.

Industry observers note that weaviate needs a server too: docker run -p 8080:8080 -p 50051:50051 cr.weaviate.io/semitechnologies/weaviate:1.34.0. Multi-vector support needs 1.29 or newer, and the embedded mode isn't available on Windows.

Defaults are enough here. Weaviate's dynamic ef resolves to 100 for a top-3 query, and this ranking is already exact from about 32 upward. That margin is a property of the embeddings rather than of Weaviate, so it's worth confirming on your own model instead of assuming the defaults hold.

Recent findings suggest that weaviate also supports MUVERA encoding, which made ingestion 3x faster and queries 1.8x faster in our test. It cost far more accuracy than that speed is worth at this size though, since the correct third passage didn't appear even in its top 50.

Vespa also runs in a container, but pyvespa starts it for you, so there's no separate docker run.

Vespa asks for the most upfront structure of the four, because you're declaring a ranking pipeline rather than just an index. In exchange you get to write MaxSim out as a tensor expression and see exactly what it computes. This version puts MaxSim in first-phase over where true, which scores all 4,874 documents and is why the output matches exhaustive MaxSim exactly. It's deliberately not what Vespa recommends at scale. Their ColBERT sample app stores int8-binarized vectors and moves MaxSim into second-phase to rerank a cheaper first stage.

Sources indicate that moving to that phased setup needs care, because second-phase rescores only the best 100 candidates by default, and here that window left two of the three correct passages unscored entirely. Raising rerank-count to cover your candidate set fixes that, though at this size the phased version still came out slower than simply scanning everything.

Late interaction is the state of the art for visual document retrieval, matching a text query against page images, with charts, tables, and layout intact, and no OCR step. This is what the ColPali family of models does, and those checkpoints load and run through the same API, with the revision pinning the open pull request that adds this one's Sentence Transformers configuration (Supported Models has the full list). Image documents are passed as URLs, local paths, or PIL images:.

Each query retrieves its own page (the diagonal), and the second query separates much more cleanly than the first, since only one of the four pages is about outlay over time.

In a recent development, the code is unchanged. Underneath, the processor handles the visual prompt and the image patches, and MaxSim scores query text tokens against document image patches. A page holds many separate regions, which is exactly what makes late interaction a natural fit here, since a single vector would have to average a chart, a table, and three paragraphs into one summary. That fidelity costs index space, though. The shapes above are 755 token vectors for one page against 25 for the query, where a Natural Questions passage from earlier averaged about 125, so token pooling is worth reaching for earlier here than it is for text.

Recent findings suggest that these are VLMs, so blueprint for the memory they need. The table in Supported Models runs from 252M to 8.8B parameters, and the small end of it stays practical on CPU where the multi-billion ones don't.

Recent findings suggest that page images are the common case, but they're not the only non-text modality. Sentence Transformers accepts text, images, audio, and video, and a checkpoint supports whichever of those its processor does, which model.modalities reports. A single document can combine modalities too, by passing a dict like {"text": ..., "image": ...} in place of a bare value. Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models covers multimodal models in Sentence Transformers more broadly, and the Usage documentation lists exactly which input formats each modality accepts.

According to recent reports, vidore/colqwen-omni-v0.1 is built on Qwen2.5-Omni and takes all four modalities. Retrieving a recorded conversation with it is the same two calls as retrieving a page:.

According to recent reports, colQwen-Omni was trained purely on image-text pairs, so its audio retrieval is zero-shot. It never heard a training example, and there is no transcription step anywhere in the pipeline. The query indicates nausea where the recording says carsickness, and it still picks the pharmacy conversation out of twenty by a wide margin.

Video works the same way, but sample the frames or it will eat your VRAM. Its release blogpost is blunt about this, that video "is very memory-intensive, so it's best suited for short clips":.

Sources indicate that at 1 fps and full resolution the same pair of videos produces 8,426 and 5,137 token vectors and peaks at 20.8 GB of VRAM, against 4,240 and 2,446 vectors and 12.5 GB here, for a model that occupies 9.0 GB on its own. The ranking is identical either way. Long audio wants the same treatment, and the release blogpost recommends 30-second chunks, which come to roughly 800 tokens each.

In a recent development, because MaxSim is a sum of per-query-token maxima, a ranking decomposes exactly, so every point of a document's score belongs to one query token and one document token. That lets you answer "why did this rank here?" precisely, rather than by eye.

For image documents, sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.interpretability overlays that decomposition onto the page as the standard ColPali heatmap, either aggregated over the query or one map per query token. Asking "How much was spent on water resources and power?" against the outlays page from above, this is where the water token went:.

heatmap.py is the runnable version, including the masking step that lines the document embedding up with the patch grid.

Text documents have no patch grid to overlay, but the same decomposition applies. text_similarity_map.py ranks a corpus and then attributes the top hit's score token by token, here on the Natural Questions corpus from earlier with the 32M-parameter mxbai-edge-colbert-v0-32m:.

rich, mond, preliminary, and final matched themselves, while when settled on since and play on game. Three special tokens contribute 22.7% of the score while carrying none of the query's content. Below this table the script prints the passage itself, with the winning tokens highlighted in place.

Recent findings suggest that if the index footprint worries you, the most effective knob is to store fewer token vectors. HierarchicalTokenPooling implements the token pooling technique from Clavié, Chaffin, and Adams by clustering each document's token vectors with Ward linkage on cosine distance and replacing each cluster with its mean, keeping roughly 1 / pool_factor of the tokens. Within one document a lot of token vectors end up close to each other, so much of what you drop is redundancy rather than signal:.

There are three places to apply it, depending on when you want to pay for it:.

By default, pooling applies to documents only, since queries are short and are the side you can't afford to distort. On the Natural Questions corpus from earlier, the reduction tracks pool_factor closely, and pooling all 608k token vectors took about 6 seconds:.

Industry observers note that A cluster mean is a worse match for a query token than the best of its members was, and the coarser the clusters, the more that shows. The original experiments measured that cost on BEIR and found very little of it, at 100.6% of the unpooled retrieval performance on average at pool_factor=2, and 99.0% at pool_factor=3. Halving your index for free is a good deal, so 2 is a reasonable place to start. How much it costs on your data is corpus-specific though, so measure it with an evaluator before you settle on a factor. The runnable comparison is token_pooling.py.

How far you can push pool_factor is also partly a property of the model. LightOn's hierarchical pooling regularization trains for exactly that, shaping the embedding space so pooling costs less and reporting 99.4% retention at 5x compression. Training with that regularizer isn't in Sentence Transformers yet, but the resulting checkpoints are ordinary PyLate models, so lightonai/LateOn-hpool-regularized loads and pools like any other.

Multi-vector models run through the same backend machinery as the rest of Sentence Transformers, so you get torch (default), onnx, and openvino, alongside half precision, Flash Attention, and torch.compile.

According to recent reports, on GPU, fp16 with Flash Attention is the best configuration we measured, at 2.44x the throughput of fp32 with no measurable retrieval quality loss. Flash Attention helps multi-vector models more than most, because documents are only truncated and never padded to a shared length, so your batches have widely varying sequence lengths that unpadding can exploit:.

Industry observers note that models with non-attend query expansion (attend=False, which covers the Stanford-NLP checkpoints like colbert-ir/colbertv2.0 and answerdotai/answerai-colbert-small-v1) reject Flash Attention at load time. Flash Attention strips attention_mask=0 positions, so the [MASK] expansion tokens that MaxSim scores would never receive an attention update. Use "sdpa" for those models.

On CPU, OpenVINO is your better bet where the architecture is supported, and int8 quantization buys a further speedup at a cost of about 0.4% accuracy. See Speeding up Inference for the full benchmark details, the export and quantization helpers, and a flowchart for picking a backend.

MultiVectorNanoBEIREvaluator runs the NanoBEIR suite of 13 small BEIR subsets with MaxSim scoring, and needs no data preparation on your side:.

This also makes it easy to check the claim from the top of this post. lightonai/LateOn and lightonai/DenseOn were trained by LightOn on the same data with the same ModernBERT backbone and the same 149M parameters, differing only in whether they keep one vector per token or pool down to one per document. Running both over all 13 NanoBEIR datasets isolates what that choice buys:.

Late interaction wins on 9 of the 13 datasets and on the mean, by roughly one NDCG point. The four it loses (ArguAna, FiQA2018, SCIDOCS, and SciFact) are the shape of the tradeoff you should expect, a real gain in retrieval quality at the same model size, paid for in index footprint, rather than a universal win on every dataset. The same pair scores 57.22 against 56.20 on the full 15-dataset BEIR, a comparable gap, so the margin is not an artifact of the small benchmark.

It has been revealed that alongside NanoBEIR, MultiVectorInformationRetrievalEvaluator, MultiVectorRerankingEvaluator, MultiVectorTripletEvaluator, and MultiVectorDistillationEvaluator cover the usual evaluation setups on your own data. They're documented in the Evaluation API Reference.

MultiVectorEncoder absorbs the modeling, inference, training, and evaluation of both libraries. Every PyLate checkpoint loads directly, and Supported Models lists the colpali-engine checkpoints along with the revision to pass where one is still needed. If you're migrating, these are the calls that change:.

Recent findings suggest that the difference worth knowing about is on bare (non-ColBERT) checkpoints, where PyLate's ColBERT("bert-base-uncased") applies the classic recipe by default while MultiVectorEncoder("bert-base-uncased") builds a plain stack, leaving the prefixes, query expansion, and skiplist as explicit choices. The training loss and evaluator equivalents, and the data-handling differences, are in the Migration Guide.

In a recent development, save compatibility is one-way in every case. PyLate, Stanford-NLP ColBERT, and colpali-engine checkpoints all load into MultiVectorEncoder, but MultiVectorEncoder.save_pretrained output isn't loadable by any of them.

Models carrying the multi-vector and sentence-transformers tags on the Hub are the list that stays current, and we're working to get those tags onto every model that works. The tables below are what we test against directly, so treat them as a starting point rather than the full set. For text retrieval in particular, any PyLate or Stanford-NLP ColBERT checkpoint loads whether or not it carries the tag yet.

In a recent development, some entries need a small Sentence Transformers configuration added to their repository first, and several of those are still open pull requests at the time of writing. Where a revision is listed below, pass it until that pull request is merged, after which the plain model name is enough:.

These load with their trained prefix tokens, query expansion, and punctuation skiplist recovered from the saved configuration.

Industry observers note that the NanoBEIR column reports the mean NDCG@10 (higher is better) across the 13 NanoBEIR datasets, each a 50-query subsample of a BEIR dataset, as a fast proxy for English text retrieval quality. We used the MultiVectorNanoBEIREvaluator to compute the scores for the primarily-English models. A - means the model was not evaluated on it. Note that NanoBEIR is a small benchmark, and its scores aren't a substitute for evaluating on your own data, which is always the right way to pick a model.

ColPali-style models embed page images as documents and text as queries.

The NanoViDoRe column reports the mean NDCG@10 (higher is better) across NanoViDoRe v3, a compact visual document retrieval benchmark spanning 8 subsets (computer science, energy, finance in English and French, HR, industrial, pharmaceuticals, and physics). Like with NanoBEIR, NanoViDoRe is a small benchmark which shouldn't replace evaluation on your own data.

Most of these are LoRA adapter repositories, with the adapter applied directly onto its base at load time. Some also have a -merged sibling on the Hub (e.g. vidore/colpali-v1.3-merged) with the adapter already folded into the weights.

It has been revealed that the three -hf entries are the transformers-native *ForRetrieval ports. They load without any configuration, but use more modeling from transformers and less from sentence_transformers. Generally, it's preferable to use the original models instead, as the ports score approximately the same.

According to recent reports, late interaction in Sentence Transformers rests on a lot of earlier work. Thanks to Omar Khattab and Matei Zaharia for ColBERT, which everything here descends from, and to the LightOn team (Antoine Chaffin, Raphael Sourty, Paulo Moura, and Amélie Chatelain) for PyLate and fast-plaid, which carried late interaction for years and shaped a good deal of the API described above.

Thanks to the ColPali team (Manuel Faysse, Hugues Sibille, Tony Wu, Bilel Omrani, Gautier Viaud, Céline Hudelot, and Pierre Colombo) for ColPali and colpali-engine, which brought late interaction to page images, and to Benjamin Clavié, Antoine Chaffin, and Griffin Adams for token pooling.

Thanks as well to the core MTEB team, Kenneth Enevoldsen and Roman Solomatin among many others, for MTEB and for the kind of hidden work that keeps information retrieval research running.

Sources indicate that and thanks to everyone who trained and released the checkpoints in Supported Models. Without them this post would have had nothing to measure.

To learn how to train or finetune these models on your own data:.

See the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multi-Vector Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers.

According to recent reports, the guide's distinction between first-stage retrieval and late-interaction reranking is useful for comparing complete systems. A practical baseline is BM25 candidate generation followed by a reranker, measuring recall at the candidate cutoff as well as final nDCG and end-to-end cost. We evaluated that pattern on a small English corpus here: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). We haven't benchmarked the multi-vector models in this guide, especially on long or visual documents, so a matched evaluation would be needed.

Google continues model chemistry experiment with Neon

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that which model to choose?
  • Google periodically tables new AI models named after elements, and its latest offering has the noble name "Neon.".
  • "Engineered for long-running agent workflows, Neon sustains performance through complex, tool-heavy tasks end-to-end — whether running standalone or acting as a fast, high-judgment Orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity," explained Koray Kavukcuoglu, SVP at Google DeepMind and chief AI architect at Google, in a blog post.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that which model to choose? It's elementary but not obvious.

Google periodically tables new AI models named after elements, and its latest offering has the noble name "Neon.".

"Engineered for long-running agent workflows, Neon sustains performance through complex, tool-heavy tasks end-to-end — whether running standalone or acting as a fast, high-judgment Orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity," explained Koray Kavukcuoglu, SVP at Google DeepMind and chief AI architect at Google, in a blog post.

Neon emerged after Google last week emitted Hydrogen, after delivering Carbon two weeks earlier and wafting Argon out the door in late September.

Unlike OpenAI's celestial more intuitive model naming scheme – Astra, Sol, Luna, and Terra – which maps celestial position to capability, Google's chemical soup doesn't suggest a specific hierarchy.

To judge by price, Carbon or Argon would be Google's top tier model, based on non-discounted price that takes effect next month, each priced at $4/M input tokens, $20/M output.

The Chocolate Factory refers to Carbon as "Our most capable reasoning model" while Argon is "Our efficient Gemini 4 frontier reasoning model … with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon across complex coding, agentic, math, and science tasks.".

Industry observers note that yet Neon, the latest element in the mix, surpasses both in Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, scoring 61 compared to Carbon at 60, Hydrogen at 54, and Argon at 50. At the same time, Neon costs less, at $3/M input tokens and $15/M output.

That favorable pricing is all the more surprising in light of Google's willingness, as of two days ago, to let users of its Gemini services opt out of generative AI model training without losing their chat histories.

Kavukcuoglu evidently recognizes the need to clarify its model rankings, an concern addressed in a blog post section titled "Where Neon sits in the Gemini 4 family.".

It has been revealed that "While Carbon tackles your hardest, long-horizon projects and Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution, Neon balances depth and efficiency," he explains. "Neon delivers frontier-level reasoning for complex, high-frequency workflows faster and more cost efficiently.".

That may not really clarify which model is appropriate for which task and frankly Google is fine with that.

According to recent reports, as noted, Google Antigravity comes with an Orchestrator that decides how to spend your money for you by swapping models on the fly. As the company describes it, a developer might start a task using Carbon, which would write a blueprint, and hand the task off to Hydrogen to benefit from its token thrift.

Antigravity does support model pinning, for those who know what they want. But Google, like other companies exploring model routing and orchestration, is fine with developers delegating decisions that affect billing to their trustworthy service provider. ®.

#46778. Industry News: How Much Memory Does Your Agent Actually Need?

📅 18 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1610 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: How Much Memory Does Your Agent Actually Need?

📅 18 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1610 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In our previous post, we compared ALTK-Evolve with ACE and revealed that how you deliver an agent's self-distilled guidelines — a few retrieved per task vs.
  • Equipping an agent with agentic memory sounds simple: distill lessons from its past work, put them back in context, and more experience should mean better performance.
  • Recent findings suggest that agentic memory is not a feature you switch on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In our previous post, we compared ALTK-Evolve with ACE and revealed that how you deliver an agent's self-distilled guidelines — a few retrieved per task vs. the whole set injected — drives both accuracy and cost. This post steps back to the question that comes before it: how much should you give it?

Equipping an agent with agentic memory sounds simple: distill lessons from its past work, put them back in context, and more experience should mean better performance. It doesn't always work that way. When we scaled the evaluation to eight models — from a 30B dense model to frontier proprietary systems — one finding stood out:.

Recent findings suggest that agentic memory is not a feature you switch on. It's a dose you calibrate to the model.

ALTK-Evolve lets an agent learn from its own past trajectories: distilling reusable guidelines and injecting them back at inference time, with no weight updates and no human annotation.

The right dose differs by model tier: strong models with headroom want the full guideline set, weaker models do best with a compact core plus per-task retrieval, and saturated models show no measurable gain.

Curated retrieval can be both the most accurate and the cheapest option: gpt-oss-120b gained +16.1pp task completion at only +5% tokens — and prompt caching keeps even the full guideline set affordable in production.

Not every model benefits from the same amount of memory. Across eight models spanning the capability spectrum, we saw three recurring patterns:.

Strong models with headroom want the full guideline set — every guideline, including rare edge-case lessons. They have the capacity to absorb and apply all of it. DeepSeek-V3.2 (671B MoE) climbed +9.5 percentage points in task completion when given its full self-mined guideline set.

According to recent reports, smaller or weaker models get drowned by a large guideline set. For these, a tight, high-confidence core plus a handful of task-relevant guidelines retrieved per task works best. gpt-oss-120b (117B MoE) gained +16.1pp with this selective approach — while the full guideline set gained less and cost ~50% more tokens.

Already-saturated models show no measurable gain. We call this the saturated pattern — the label describes what we observed, not a proven cause. The model may already have been near its ceiling on these tasks, the guidelines may not have addressed its remaining failures, or it may not have applied the guidance effectively. GLM-5 (745B MoE) sat here in our runs.

It has been revealed that what puts a model into one pattern rather than another isn't simply parameter count. Benchmark headroom, context-window size, architecture, guideline quality, and task distribution all appear to shape where a model lands, and separating those factors is ongoing work. The practical takeaway holds either way: the right dose of memory depends on the model, and we can calibrate it.

"Memory" here doesn't mean replaying a past transcript. It means a guideline set — strategies that worked, mistakes to avoid, and edge cases — distilled from the agent's own prior trajectories. The loop is straightforward:.

The agent attempts tasks and produces trajectories.

ALTK-Evolve extracts behavioral guidelines from both its successful and unsuccessful runs.

It consolidates those guidelines into a reusable set.

At inference time, the agent receives either the full guideline set or a task-relevant selection of it.

Industry observers note that no model weights are updated. The learning loop changes the guidance available to the agent, not the underlying model — which is exactly why it's cheap to adopt and portable across the eight models we tested.

It has been revealed that we evaluated on AppWorld — 585 multi-step tasks (168 test_normal + 417 test_challenge) across 9 simulated apps (calendars, messaging, payments, and so on). Tasks are scored two ways: whether the agent fully completes each task (TGC — Task Goal Completion) and whether every variant of a scenario passes (SGC — Scenario Goal Completion, a stricter, all-or-nothing bar). Full definitions are in the appendix.

Because the confusing part of any memory study is what's actually in the context window, we define the configurations up front.

Both memory configurations draw from the same guideline set, mined once (via the loop above) from AppWorld's training split only. What changes between them is only how that one set is delivered — the full guideline set injects all of it every step, while curated retrieval delivers a selected subset — never how the guidelines were produced, and no test-split data ever goes into building it.

The number of guidelines a model mines depends on its own capability, so we report configurations by strategy — "full guideline set" vs. "curated retrieval" — rather than by raw counts, which aren't comparable across models.

Representative models from the eight-model sweep, measured by task completion (TGC) on test_normal:.

Figure 1. Representative models in the three observed patterns. Bars show TGC on AppWorld test_normal for baseline vs. the best-memory configuration; the x-axis begins at 40% to make differences visible. TGC alone understates the larger SGC gains — see the SGC columns in the table below.

The figure plots TGC to keep it readable; the table adds the stricter SGC metric, where the gains are often larger:.

Reading the SGC column, the stricter metric usually moves more than TGC — DeepSeek's SGC jumps +16.1pp against a +9.5pp TGC gain — because good guidelines especially help an agent clear every variant of a scenario, not just the average case. And the effect doesn't disappear at the top of the range: GPT-5.5 and Opus, both near the ceiling on TGC, still gain +7.2 and +7.1pp SGC respectively. Memory keeps paying off as long as a model has a remaining failure mode to target.

A practical concern: injecting a full guideline set inflates every ReAct step's input, because the guidelines are re-sent each turn. Here's what we observed:.

Recent findings suggest that table 1. Average token use per task, accumulated across agent steps, measured against the no-memory baseline.

In a recent development, curated retrieval keeps cost near baseline. For weaker models, where selection wins on accuracy, it also wins on cost — the best of both worlds (+16.1pp TGC at only +5% tokens for gpt-oss-120b). Better performance here does not require more inference cost.

Memory doesn't blow up the reasoning loop. DeepSeek runs about the same number of ReAct steps with memory as without (≈18–19 on average), so the added cost is input-token inflation, not longer trajectories.

The real efficiency lever in production is prompt caching: the static portion of the guideline set is identical across steps and can be cached, cutting effective cost substantially. Cache-aware prompt design — keeping the shared guideline-set prefix stable so it stays cacheable — is worth engineering for. We also hypothesize that context-window size plays a role: models with larger windows may absorb the full guideline set more effectively, while smaller-context models benefit more from retrieval that keeps injected content compact. We have not yet run controlled experiments isolating this factor.

It has been revealed that the lesson isn't to give an agent everything it has learned. It's to give it the amount of experience it can actually use.

For weak models, that means a compact core plus a few task-specific lessons — which, conveniently, is also the cheapest option.

For strong models with headroom, it means preserving the full guideline set, kept affordable in production via prompt caching.

For saturated models, it means spending no extra context until their remaining failure modes are better understood.

The gains are real across the board — automatic, leakage-free, and requiring no human annotation — but only when the dose fits the model.

This is a starting point, not the finish line:.

According to recent reports, A learned selector. Our current retrieval ranks guidelines by cosine similarity, which we've shown doesn't perfectly predict which guidelines help a given task. A selector trained on outcome signal is the natural next step.

Memory for very weak models. Below a minimum capability baseline, self-distillation lacks signal. Teacher-distilled memory for very weak models is a separate problem we're exploring.

Beyond AppWorld. These results are validated on AppWorld — a rigorous multi-step benchmark, but a single one. Broader agent benchmarks and real-world deployments are in progress.

Industry observers note that isolating context window. As above, we want controlled experiments that separate context-window size from raw capability.

Try the ALTK-Evolve library — which includes the extraction, consolidation, and retrieval pipeline used here — or read the full technical report for the complete method and ablations.

AppWorld tasks are graded by two metrics, both reported as percentages (higher is better):.

In a recent development, TGC — Task Goal Completion. The share of individual tasks the agent completes fully and correctly. This is the headline "did it get the job done" number.

Industry observers note that SGC — Scenario Goal Completion. A stricter, all-or-nothing metric. Each scenario bundles several variants of the same task (the same request with different data, phrasing, or edge conditions). SGC counts a scenario as passing only if the agent succeeds on every variant. It measures reliability — an agent that solves a task most of the time but fails on one variant scores on TGC but not on SGC.

In a recent development, really interesting take on agentic memory. The idea that memory needs to be calibrated to the model rather than simply accumulated is especially useful for production systems. Selective retrieval also seems like a practical way to improve reliability without unnecessarily increasing context and inference costs. It makes a strong case for thoughtful custom AI agent development and enterprise AI agent solutions, where memory, performance, and cost all need to be designed together. https://mobisoftinfotech.com/services/ai-agent-development-tech giant.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I’ve been bashing on updating this site’s design for the last couple of weeks. It’s high time things get a fresh coat of paint, right? The last version of CSS-Tricks was pushed five years ago. That’s ancient in web (and dog) years.

It’s not like the site has simply sat all that time. We pushed lots of changes and shipped new features, particularly since 2024, but we never really got the paint brushes out of storage.

Now, before there’s a chorus of “things don’t look thaaaat different” I want to say I’m rarely a fan of complete re-builds and tend to lean into iterative releases. And the new v20 theme is what I’d call an iterative rollup that’s worthy of a version bump.

Let’s go over the most notable updates to see why.

According to recent reports, first and foremost, some of the biggest changes are what you don’t see. As you might imagine, this site has carried over plenty of pieces across 19 years. I decided to excavate the theme and definitely found some ghosts to bust.

For example, the global compiled JavaScript file retained some scripts that just weren’t being used anymore. Things like handling embedded versions of the newsletter from before we began self-hosting the posts. There were relics that catered specifically to the Flexbox Guide for handling toggles back before we had proper HTML . There was a jQuery lazy-loader thing that is well-covered by WordPress core now. We had some scripts for serving third-party ads that are no longer needed now that we’re self-hosting ads. Things like that. The overall JavaScript was nicely trimmed from 151.6 KB (55.3 KB gzipped) to 133.8 KB (48.1 KB).

According to recent reports, I also decided to formally retire the CSS-Tricks Forum. We put it in “archive mode” back in, like, 2018. None of those discussions are particularly valuable for today as they were over 10 years ago, so I deactivated the bbPress plugin that powered it and cleared out the database… and wow, that carved a whopping 400 MB from the ol’ database, not to mention it allowed me to drop several custom templates from the theme.

There were more ghosts busted along the way and, to be sure, there are still some lurking around. But it’s way less scary poking around the theme directory now, and further cleanup should be a lot easier from here on out.

It has been revealed that yeah, yeah, raise your hand if you’re still running Gulp. We are 🙋‍♂️. That’s not a bad thing in and of itself, but keeping it in a fixed state for all this time is not the greatest. I think we’re sporting a more modern workflow than before, even if there’s still room to grow. A smattering of the related commits:.

For years, I endured the same errors every time I fired up a new terminal. Those are gone and things run super cleanly, not to mention quickly. Very happy here.

Sources indicate that oof, this is everyone’s favorite job, right?! Aside from being able to spot and fix a few unescaped custom field calls here and there, I decided to ask Claude to help me with a holistic audit. I prompted it to review recent WordPress security release notes and identify areas where the theme could be hardened to comply with what WordPress is doing.

Sources indicate that whoa, you used AI? Yeah, I sure did. But for things like this where it could be my little gopher and allow me more time to do what I do best: front-end. I’m still able to make most of the patches myself based on the output recommendations, but it’s nice to have a gut-check for things where I’m clearly no expert, like security.

I still use and like Sass very much. I mean, yes, I would like to be straight-up vanilla CSS everywhere, but I can’t tear myself away from partials in particular.

The previous theme had a fairly nice “flat” structure — very few partial directories and most things all in the same top-level source. Totally cool. But an organization nut like me (you should see my house) has to have a place for everything to live. It ain’t perfect, but I’m happy with what I was able to put together without leveling the building in the process.

There are some compromises. Like, /header should really be in /layout. The ordering is really crucial, though, and some of my ideals were simply not possible. I’m hoping to eventually work in some sort of Cascade Layers structure.

Sources indicate that I’m pleased as punch to see the overall size of CSS drop in the process. It went from 180 KB (31.7 KB) to 169 KB (24.6 KB). Not hugely significant, but not not significant either. I had to do a couple tricky things to cheat my way there, like serving all the form styles I’m about to talk about into a separate forms.css file and serving it just on pages where WooCommerce, Restrict Content Pro, and Gravity Forms are enqueued.

Recent findings suggest that are you starting to notice a trend? We’re still talking about fairly invisible work. CSS-Tricks has so many nooks and crannies that it’s nearly impossible to make things perfectly consistent across the board. But because of those nooks and crannies, so many fixed values, magic numbers, one-off styles, and older utilities were hiding about. I decided to tackle a good chunk of that while reorganizing the Sass.

It has been revealed that for example, there are now semantic design tokens that abstract away one-off colors. So many grays, let me tell you. Now there’s a maintainable palette that’s referenced throughout. Same with fonts, font styles, and font sizes. Same with paddings and margins. It feels a lot better to make a change at the “system” level with confidence that the change is taking effect everywhere it needs to.

It has been revealed that but this is also where some clearly visible changes happened! Most notably, link styles are consistent all over the place with a small handful of intended and maintained variations. Not only is it more pleasing visually, but it improves accessibility throughout because the inherited styles default to proper visual cues that do not rely solely on color or opacity changes.

It has been revealed that oh, and my favorite piece of this? Forms and tables have both been redone. That’s tough to do in a WordPress theme where these components don’t always come from one source. For example, forms could come from any one of the Gravity Forms, WooCommerce, or Restrict Content Pro plugins, and they all have their own stylesheets. Resetting those allowed me to bring a certain level of harmony in all those instances.

According to recent reports, OK, something even more visual. This is the first time CSS-Tricks has had more than one color scheme! It certainly could have been done a long time ago, but I’d also argue that the design hasn’t really called for a light/dark toggle over the last 8 years or so. It’s a nice blend of both light and dark elements that marry the best of both worlds no matter your theme preference.

Recent findings suggest that but I had to take a stab, right? The site has predominantly been dark despite the content being against a white background, so I treated things as though a “dark” mode already existed. The result is a creamy light theme that is largely just a change in background and component styles. And I used some of what I learned from the recent “toggle” debate to handle system, dark, and light themes with a single toggle.

In a recent development, what hasn’t changed is the main content container you see in things like articles. That was already white, even in a “dark” mode, and I’m not confident that simply toggling it between white and black is the best approach. Something on the radar for sure.

Oh, and it’s all wired up to a view transition that slides the new theme over the previous one.

According to recent reports, I hope you think the site’s header and footer are cute. Yes, cute. That’s what I was going for when adding a colorful series of dots as the backdrop.

Sorta like a subtle candy texture, right? Or a colorful group of stars? I dunno, but I’m calling it “Jawbreaker” for lack of a better term and because it reminds me of the jawbreaker candy I loved as a kid. Naming still sucks.

It’s all part of the same SVG. I really, really (really) wanted to random()-ly position dots around, but that would have taken a lot of empty individual elements (e.g., ) in the markup. Not my favorite. So, I generate the elements in PHP:.

I really, really wanted to random()-ize all the things, but inlining random coordinates on each was the way to go. Same deal with the inlined styles that set a fill, and sizing for each circle in the texture, and variables that set a --delay and --dur on the subtle animation that twinkles them in and out.

I’ll have to look at generating the SVG using or whatever later since that pattern repeats in the footer, too.

That’s carried through to the 404 page as well:.

Recent findings suggest that if your browser supports border-shape and random() (only Chrome, I think), then the homepage gives you a blobby-blob shape behind the grid of author avatars. Hover it and it gets, you know, even blobbier.

It takes an existing pattern I’m calling .gradient-card:.

…and sets a gradient on the component’s :before pseudo:.

That sits underneath the :after pseudo that’s translucent, allowing the :before‘s gradient to show through a smidge:.

It has been revealed that the differing border-radius values allow :before to bleed outside, giving the impression of a border around the entire deal. That’s the basic shape. The border-shape is where things get blobby:.

It has been revealed that those variables? They’re mapped to shape()s. I grabbed the first one from Temani Afif’s blob generator:.

Sources indicate that it’s called “static” because that’s the default state. Hover or focus on the component and it swaps out those points out with a “hover” version of the shape:.

Those variables? They’re mapped to random() values:.

According to recent reports, so, the hover state is different on each page load. And we animate between the two:.

I’m pretty stoked on this one. The Almanac has grown, evolved, and just plain gotten great the past few years. But the primary page for it… not so great. It was definitely overshadowed by work on the pages inside it and never revisited beyond clickable cards to get to each feature subset.

It has been revealed that now the page is a real index of the CSS features that gets you where you need to go swiftly. Someone somewhere sometime did some sort of CSS periodic table. I forget where I’d seen that but the general idea sat with me and I thought I could pull it off. There’s nothing “tricky” about it but I love what the layout adds to the overall site.

It has been revealed that this is another area that sorely needed love. Our guides have always been a vertical stack of items. The book effect was definitely cool, but I started believing that leaning on it as the main visual hook was holding things back from being more functional. With something like 27 guides, we’re talking about a lot of scrolling with no clear idea of what you’re going to see as you go.

Again, nothing “tricky” but I like the overall usefulness of the latest layout. There’s a featured guide, a widget of newly added and updated guides, and a categorized grid of everything below that.

The pages that show all of an author’s published articles got a little spruce-up, too.

It’s a little change, really. The right sidebar was moved to the left and the author image and bio moved in, allowing the articles to creep up to the top. I hope to do more here since the small layout tweak opens up more opportunities.

Also need to do the larger Authors index, but another time.

This one’s just for those of us working in the WordPress editor. I don’t need a complete visual editor to get things done, but it is a nice affordance to have some of the front-end styles sneak into the editing UI for a better idea of what you’re working with.

Using Lighthouse to measure things like performance, accessibility, and best practices is woefully fraught with caveats, but there’s no reason to chuck it completely. I find them more fun than fact and I don’t mind the recommendations for improving things.

So, after a few runs and tweaks, here’s how things shook out theme-to-theme.

In a recent development, I’m happy here. There are some things I just don’t have the control to fix when it comes to performance, so seeing v20 come in consistent with v19 is just fine by me. I’m happier with the boosts to accessibility and best practices. SEO? Meh. Don’t really care unless it’s hurting more key things like accessibility.

Again, very happy. There’s little I can do with time to first byte but everything else seems to clock in at least marginally better. The total page weight is a clear win and that’s probably what I care most about here.

It has been revealed that oh gosh, there’s a lot more but they’re mostly minor things that don’t bubble up to the front end. Sort of the same way browser changelogs have some generic line of “bug squashing” or whatever. In this case, it’s things like better post queries and breadcrumbs and function management and naming and… you get it.

There’s definitely so much more to do. And plenty of things I’m sure I missed or broke along the way. That’s just life and those will have to come in another iterative release less worthy of a version bump. You can let me know what I muffed up in the comments.

I hope you at least like where this is going!
